Just the sticky vinyl seat of the bus home,  
the way my hair smelled like fry oil and dust,  
and how, sometimes, when the AC died  
in August, I’d press my forehead  
against the cool glass of the breakroom window,  
watching the parking lot shimmer,  
thinking nothing at all—  
just the hum, the heat, the slow drip  
of the leaky faucet behind the sink,  
counting seconds between drops  
like it mattered.

title: free verse poem|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
I. The Last Watch  
The brass clock ticks slower now—  
not broken, just reluctant.  
I polish the lens one more time,  
fingertips tracing the cold, curved glass,  
smearing breath where salt once etched its map.  
Outside, the sea hums its old complaint,  
and the beam cuts clean through fog—  
a silver blade I’ve swung for forty years.  
Tonight, it feels less like a warning  
and more like a farewell I’m not allowed to speak.

II. Packing Light  
Boxes wait in the keeper’s room:  
a chipped mug, a coil of frayed rope,  
letters tied with blue twine—  
all signed *Home, someday*.  
I leave the logbook open on the desk,  
last entry ink still damp:  
*Wind NW, 28 knots. Light steady.*  
No mention of the hollow behind my ribs,  
or how the stairs groan louder tonight,  
as if the tower itself is holding its breath.

III. Unlatching  
At dawn, I turn the final key—  
not in the door, but in the lamp’s heart:  
the wick lowers, the flame shrinks,  
then blinks out like a tired eye.  
Silence rushes in, thick and sudden,  
filling spaces the light used to hold.  
I step down the spiral,  
leaving the lantern dark,  
leaving the sea to keep its own watch—  
and carry, in my pocket,  
one warm lens shard,  
still catching the first true light.

title: pantoum|a beekeeper in winter
text:
Winter's Honeyed Silence

In the hush of winter, bees cluster in warmth,
A beekeeper wanders through the silent snow.
His breath a cloud, thoughts as quiet as the swarm,
Dreaming of spring, when the meadows will glow.

A beekeeper wanders through the silent snow,
Inspecting hives with a careful, gentle hand.
Dreaming of spring, when the meadows will glow,
He hears the soft hum, life's steadfast band.

Inspecting hives with a careful, gentle hand,
His breath a cloud, thoughts as quiet as the swarm.
He hears the soft hum, life's steadfast band,
In the hush of winter, bees cluster in warmth.

title: ode|the stars seen from a desert
text:
Ode to the Desert Stars, Not Heaven’s Jewelry Box  

Not pinpricks. Not diamond dust flung careless by a bored god.  
These are *burns*: cold plasma scars on the black leather of night—  
each one a wound left open, raw and unblinking,  
spilling ultraviolet light you can’t see but *feel*  
as static prickle on the back of your throat.  

That smear? Not “Milky Way.” A smear is what’s left  
after you wipe greasy thumbprints off a diner window  
at 3 a.m.—this is *that*: luminous grime,  
a billion suns’ exhaust, thick as spilled motor oil,  
glinting where it catches the thin, dry wind.  

The North Star? Not steady. It *shivers*,  
a heat-haze tremor above cracked clay,  
like the single bulb in a broken-down truck stop sign—  
flickering, not faithful. Its light took 433 years  
to reach this patch of sand where your boot sinks  
an inch, then stops, held by ancient silt.  

And the silence isn’t empty. It *rings*:  
the high, thin whine of distant coyotes tuning up,  
the grit-scrape of a sidewinder’s belly dragging east,  
the slow *pop-pop* of cooling basalt under your palm—  
all of it humming *under* the stars, not beneath them.  

You don’t wish on them.  
You watch how their light, after 2,000 years,  
still lands sharp as shattered bottle glass  
on the edge of a rusted soda can half-buried near your heel—  
proof not of eternity, but of *distance*:  
how long it takes for fire to become a scratch  
on the surface of the world.

title: short lyric poem|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
Dawn’s First Sip  

Steam curls—a silver thread—  
in the hush before light,  
before birds stitch the sky with sound,  
before the world remembers its name.  

Dark brew, bitter and deep,  
warming palms like a secret held too long.  
The mug’s quiet heat,  
the clock’s soft breath,  
the window bluing at the edges—  

I am the first awake,  
and the coffee is my silent vow:  
to hold this stillness,  
just a little longer,  
just until the light  
touches the rim of the cup.

title: ghazal|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
By the old pier, dawn whispers through misty veils,
My uncle casts lines, silence his only tale.

We watch ripples dance on water's cool skin,
His hands, worn by years, steady as a violin.

Eagles cry overhead, nature’s symphony plays,
In his quiet world, he drifts through the haze.

Sometimes I wonder what secrets he keeps,
Locked away in his chest, like treasures deep.

The sun climbs, casting gold on silent shores,
Our shadows stretch long, time gently implores.

A fish leaps, silver flash against the light,
He smiles, a rare glimpse, then fades from sight.

Here, in this moment, words seem almost rude,
Just the lapping waves and the gentle brood.

title: elegy|an abandoned railway station
text:
Elegy for the Station at Hollow Creek

The ticket window gapes—a hollow eye,  
its glass long gone, its frame bleached bare by rain and years.  
Beneath the eaves, where sparrows stitch the air with flight,  
a rusted clock hangs frozen at 4:17—  
not morning, not evening, just absence wearing time like ash.

Planks of the platform sag like tired spines;  
lichen writes slow psalms on cracked concrete.  
A single bench remains—not wood, but ghostwood,  
its green paint flaking into pollen-dust  
that trembles when the wind remembers a train.

No whistle now—only the hush  
that gathers in the throat of the tunnel mouth,  
dark and damp as an unspoken name.  
Weeds rise through the rails—not wild, but witness:  
tall grasses bowing where iron once held breath,  
where steam once rose like a vow, then vanished.

I stand where passengers stood—  
hands gripping worn leather satchels,  
eyes scanning horizons that no longer answer.  
The timetable’s gone. The signals sleep.  
Even the pigeons have learned the grammar of departure:  
they circle once, then choose another sky.

What lingers isn’t ruin—it’s resonance:  
the echo of footsteps swallowed by gravel,  
the warmth still held in brick at dusk,  
the way light falls, exact and tender,  
on the empty space where “WELCOME” used to gleam.

This is not an ending.  
It is silence learning how to hold a name—  
Hollow Creek, Hollow Creek—  
until the earth, soft and certain,  
takes back the rails, the roof, the waiting,  
and sings them, slowly, into root.

title: pantoum|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
Silent Reel

The river bends where cattails sigh,  
My uncle sits without a word,  
His weathered hands know how to tie  
Each knot the quiet water heard.  

My uncle sits without a word,  
A rod held steady, still and low—  
Each knot the quiet water heard,  
The line slips soft as breath below.  

A rod held steady, still and low,  
His eyes trace ripples, deep and slow—  
The line slips soft as breath below,  
No need for speech; the current knows.  

His eyes trace ripples, deep and slow,  
The bobber dips—a sudden pull—  
No need for speech; the current knows,  
He lifts the silver, strong and full.  

The bobber dips—a sudden pull—  
The river bends where cattails sigh—  
He lifts the silver, strong and full,  
My uncle sits without a word.

title: ode|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
In the quiet hum of Sunday's pause,  
where whispers thread through sunlit air,  
a library stands, its walls a fortress,  
guarding dreams in rows of spines.  

Here, the dust motes dance like tiny planets,  
orbiting slow around the glow of lamps,  
each one a universe held in soft hands,  
pages turning, worlds colliding, silent.

A woman with eyes like old maps,  
traces routes on paper continents,  
her fingers charting paths unseen,  
while outside, the world forgets to breathe.

The children, small explorers, huddle,  
in corners where light pools like gold,  
their laughter a secret code, deciphered  
only by the wise and the very young.

Books lie open, mouths agape,  
telling tales of shadow and light,  
of heroes with hearts of iron,  
and villains who dream in shades of gray.

In this cathedral of quiet thought,  
even the clocks seem to hesitate,  
as if time itself were a fragile thing,  
held together by the weight of words.

And there, by the window, an old man sits,  
his face a map of years and stories,  
eyes closed, but not asleep—listening,  
to the symphony of silence, the rustle of leaves.  

Outside, the city stirs, a gentle beast,  
but here, in this sanctuary, time is a river,  
flowing slow, deep, and wide,  
carrying all who enter, far from the noise.

title: villanelle|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
The Smell of a Grandmother’s Kitchen  

Cinnamon swirls in warm, forgiving air,  
A golden crust just pulled from oven’s hold,  
Where time dissolves like sugar, soft and rare.  

The kettle sighs; its steam begins to flare,  
While dill and thyme on worn wood surfaces fold—  
Cinnamon swirls in warm, forgiving air.  

Old linen napkins, folded with such care,  
Still bear the ghost of lavender and old  
Where time dissolves like sugar, soft and rare.  

Bread cools on racks, its yeasty breath laid bare,  
And jam jars gleam like rubies, deep and cold—  
Cinnamon swirls in warm, forgiving air.  

Her hands, though knotted, move without compare,  
Kneading memory into dough’s bright gold—  
Where time dissolves like sugar, soft and rare.  

No clock ticks here—just scent, and love, and prayer,  
A sanctuary no sorrow can control:  
Cinnamon swirls in warm, forgiving air,  
Where time dissolves like sugar, soft and rare.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
The ridge-line’s bleeding orange—no, not quite red—  
just that cheap rust-paint they used on Dad’s old shed  
before the hail took half the roof instead.  
I’m chewing gum, stale spearmint, stuck and dead  
between my molars. Car’s AC wheezes, weak,  
blowing warm air that smells like burnt toast crust.  
My left knee’s throbbing where the fence post peeked  
through last fall’s mud—still hasn’t lost its trust  
in gravity. Smoke’s not smoke, really—more  
like breath held too long by a tired lung,  
a slow exhale you almost ignore  
until it’s thick enough to taste, to sting.  
That one pine’s still standing, black but whole,  
while everything else just… stops being coal.

title: blank verse meditation|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
The phone rings, a sudden intrusion in the stillness,
A voice from years ago, across miles and mountains.
"Hello," he says, as if no time has passed,
As if we last spoke just yesterday, not decades back.

I close my eyes, and the room fades, replaced
By memories of childhood summers, barefoot on grass,
Chasing fireflies under a sky vast and deep,
Laughter echoing, unburdened by the weight of tomorrow.

He speaks of his life, a tapestry of moments,
Threads of joy and sorrow, woven with care.
I picture him, lines etched on his face,
Hands that once built sandcastles, now hold the world's wear.

A pause, and the silence between us grows,
Like the chasm of years, yet filled with an unspoken bond.
We are brothers, connected by blood and by dreams,
Separated by distance, but never truly apart.

He tells me of his children, their laughter and tears,
How they remind him of our own shared past.
I see them, young faces, a new generation,
Carrying forward the legacy of our family's love.

As the call ends, a bittersweet farewell,
I am left with the echoes of his voice,
A reminder of the ties that bind, even in absence,
A bridge over time, a link to the boy I once knew.

The room returns, the stillness reclaimed,
But my heart is full, a warmth that lingers.
A phone call, a connection, a moment of grace,
In the quiet, a brother found, and a soul renewed.

title: villanelle|hope after a long illness
text:
I. The First Light  

The light returns, though faint and thin and slow,  
A tremor in the wrist, a breath held deep—  
The world outside begins to softly glow.  

No longer bound by fever’s cruel tableau,  
Each dawn arrives with promises to keep;  
The light returns, though faint and thin and slow.  

The mirror shows a face I barely know—  
Eyes hollowed, yet no longer lost in sleep—  
The world outside begins to softly glow.  

The clock ticks not as threat, but as a flow  
Of time reclaimed, no longer steeped in grief;  
The light returns, though faint and thin and slow.  

I trace the wall where shadows used to grow—  
Now dust motes dance where stillness used to creep.  
The world outside begins to softly glow.  

This fragile warmth—I will not let it go.  
It is enough. It is the vow I keep:  
The light returns, though faint and thin and slow,  
The world outside begins to softly glow.  

II. The Unfurling  

A hand unclenches—not in strength, but grace,  
A sparrow hops where ivy starts to climb;  
Hope is the quiet pulse behind the face.  

The garden gate hangs open in its place,  
And dandelions pierce the cracked front line—  
A hand unclenches—not in strength, but grace.  

I taste the air—not medicine, but space,  
Not silence, but the chime of distant time;  
Hope is the quiet pulse behind the face.  

The chair beside me holds no ghostly trace,  
Just sunlight pooled like honey, warm and prime;  
A hand unclenches—not in strength, but grace.  

I name each bird that lands without a trace,  
Each petal drifting, unafraid, sublime;  
Hope is the quiet pulse behind the face.  

This breath is mine. This moment has its place.  
No need for proof. No need to count the rhyme:  
A hand unclenches—not in strength, but grace,  
Hope is the quiet pulse behind the face.  

III. The Steady Flame  

Not fire—but steady, low, and clear and true,  
A candle lit when all the winds had ceased;  
Hope is the flame that learns to burn anew.  

It does not shout, nor blaze in sudden hue,  
Nor promise skies restored or sorrows eased—  
Not fire—but steady, low, and clear and true.  

It flickers, yes—but never lets wind undo  
The shape it holds, the warmth it will not cease;  
Hope is the flame that learns to burn anew.  

I watch it hold the dark, not overcome,  
A small, sure grammar only patience reads;  
Not fire—but steady, low, and clear and true.  

No need for wings—just presence, calm, and room,  
Just hands that rest, at last, in folded peace;  
Hope is the flame that learns to burn anew.  

This light is earned. This light belongs to you.  
It asks no more than this: to tend, believe—  
Not fire—but steady, low, and clear and true,  
Hope is the flame that learns to burn anew.

title: sequence of haiku|teenage summer jobs
text:
Lawnmower Blues  
Blade’s dull whine—  
a beetle’s iridescent shell  
spits from the chute.  

Diner Shift  
Coffee steam rises,  
then vanishes—just like the tip  
left in a napkin.  

Pool Lifeguard  
Chlorine stings my eyes,  
but the real burn is watching  
her flip-flops sink slow  
in the deep-end drain.  

Fast-Food Drive-Thru  
Static crackle: *“Double cheese, no pickles.”*  
I press the mic—  
my thumb leaves a greasy crescent  
on the plastic.  

Bookstore Stockroom  
Dust motes swirl in the loading dock light.  
A paperback spine cracks open—  
*“The End”* printed sideways  
on the cut edge.

title: spoken-word poem|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Autumn Leaves in a Cemetery

In the silence of stone and shadow, where whispers tread,
Lies a tapestry woven by the hands of the dead.
Golden leaves, like memories, softly fall,
Each one a story, a silent call.

They carpet paths that few dare walk,
Underneath the watchful gaze of an ancient clock.
Time ticks on, yet here it seems to pause,
Caught between the branches, in the quiet cause.

Crimson, amber, and gold, they blend,
A symphony of colors, without end.
On graves they rest, as if to say,
"Even in death, beauty has its way."

The wind, a gentle undertaker, stirs,
Carrying secrets, hopes, and fears.
Through the air, these leaves do dance,
In this place, they find their chance.

To remind us all, who come and go,
That life, like seasons, ebbs and flows.
From vibrant green to fiery red,
Then back to earth, from which we're fed.

Here, among the fallen, we see
Reflections of our own mortality.
Yet, in each leaf, there's also grace,
A reminder of love, not just of space.

So let the autumn leaves in this hallowed ground,
Speak of peace, where sorrow is found.
For in their fleeting, fragile show,
Is the eternal cycle, ebb and flow.

title: sequence of haiku|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
Left glove on the fence post—  
blue wool, thumb split at the seam,  
my mother’s hand-me-down.  

Rain last night: the cuff’s stiff  
with dried mud and one bent pin  
I dropped fixing the latch.  

Wind tugs at the fingers.  
A sparrow landed there twice—  
didn’t stay. Just looked.

title: spoken-word poem|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
V-Formation Over Black Ice  

Listen—  
not to the wind, but to the *absence* of it:  
that hollow hush where breath freezes mid-air,  
where the lake isn’t water anymore—  
it’s a slab of shattered obsidian,  
veined with cold-blue cracks,  
holding its breath beneath three inches of ice.  

And then—  
a tremor in the sky.  
Not sound first.  
*Shadow.*  
A slow, dark stitch unraveling across the white.  

They come—not flying *over*,  
but *through* the silence,  
wings knifing air so still it rings like glass.  
Twenty-seven geese.  
Maybe thirty.  
I count by throat—each honk a raw, brass note  
bounced off the frozen surface below,  
doubling back, thin and ancient,  
as if the lake remembers every call ever made above it.  

Watch how their V dips—  
not for warmth (there is none),  
not for rest (the ice offers no shore),  
but for *truth*:  
the lead goose tilts her wing just so,  
and the one behind catches her updraft—  
a shared breath, a shared burden,  
a geometry of trust written in muscle and migration.  

Below them, the ice groans—  
a low, tectonic sigh—  
and for one suspended second,  
the reflection fractures:  
twenty-seven black Vs shiver in the dark,  
as if the sky and the deep are arguing  
over who holds the real flock.  

They don’t look down.  
They can’t.  
Their eyes are fixed on the latitude of light,  
on the green memory of marshes not yet thawed,  
on the unbroken line of *forward*.  

But I do look down.  
At the ice.  
At the shadows.  
At the space between the wings and the water—  
that fragile, humming inch of air  
where cold and courage meet,  
where survival is not a destination,  
but the act of staying airborne  
while the world turns hard and silent beneath you.  

They vanish west.  
The V dissolves into cloud-edge.  
The lake exhales—  
a plume of mist rising, thin and silver,  
as if the water, too,  
just remembered how to breathe.

title: free verse poem|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
Whispers of Smoke

Distant hills murmur in gray,
Silent voices rise and sway.
A story told by the wind's soft play,
Where trees once stood, now shadows fray.

Glow Against the Night

Orange tendrils lick the sky,
A dance of flames, so wild and high.
The stars dim as the fire sighs,
Casting light where darkness lies.

Ashes to the Wind

Morning breaks with a hazy eye,
What was fierce, now gently dies.
Scattered embers, whispers fly,
In the calm, the forest cries.

title: blank verse meditation|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The Last Watch  

The lamp still burns, though I have wound the clock  
And checked the wick one final time—its flame  
A steady, silvered tongue against the dark.  
Outside, the sea exhales in ragged gusts,  
A low and ancient voice that knows no name,  
No mercy, no farewell. The glass is cold  
Beneath my palm, the brass rail worn smooth  
By decades of this same slow, salt-stung hand.  
I trace the cracks in mortar near the sill—  
Each one a year, a storm, a letter lost,  
A child’s first word received by lantern-light,  
A wife’s last breath dissolved in fog so thick  
It muffled even grief. The logbook lies  
Open on the desk: entries precise, sparse—  
*Wind NW, force six. Fog bank thick at dawn.  
Lens polished. Oil level nominal.*  
No mention of the hollow in the chest  
That deepens with each turning of the key,  
No record of the way the gulls tonight  
Cry sharper, as if sensing vacancy.  
I climb the spiral—step by iron step—  
Past ghosts of duty, past the weight of years  
That coil like rope around the heart’s dry core.  
At the top, the beam cuts clean and white and far,  
A blade of certainty in shifting air.  
It sweeps the waves, the rocks, the empty shore—  
Still faithful, though the keeper stays no more.  
I do not turn it off. I let it burn.  
Let light outlive the hand that lit it first.  
The tide rolls in. The bell buoy chimes.  
I stand—and wait—not for the dawn, but for  
The quiet after. The unblinking eye  
Still open, long after the watcher’s gone.

title: ghazal|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
The Four Seasons of an Orchard

Blossoms blush—spring’s breath, a trembling vow,  
Then summer swells, and heavy branches bow.  

Green fruit hangs low where bees hum lullabies,  
While twilight pools in shade—no thought of how.  

Autumn arrives with amber, crisp and slow,  
Each fallen pear a soft, unspoken vow.  

The wind strips bare the boughs, yet holds no blame—  
It sings the same old song it sang before.  

Winter comes: frost etches silver lace,  
A silent orchard dreams beneath the snow.  

Though roots remember warmth, though soil still waits,  
No season stays—yet all return, somehow.

title: blank verse meditation|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Beneath the whispering arms of ancient oaks,
The leaves, a tapestry of gold and rust,
Flutter down like thoughts too heavy to keep.
I wander through this silent, hallowed ground,
Where names etched in stone speak of lives long past—
Eleanor, 1923-1987, beloved mother,
Her plot adorned with plastic flowers, faded,
Yet somehow more real than the fresh-cut blooms
Laid at the foot of a newer grave nearby.

The air is crisp, a hint of winter’s bite,
And I, in my worn coat, feel every chill.
These leaves, they crumble underfoot, a sound
So soft, it’s almost like a secret shared
Between the earth and sky. A squirrel darts,
Gathering its harvest, indifferent
To the solemnity that holds me here.

I think of all the stories buried deep,
The loves, the losses, the unspoken dreams.
A gust stirs, and the leaves dance, wild and free,
For just a moment, before they settle once more,
A fleeting echo of life’s restless pulse.

title: ghazal|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
Ghazal for the Driver’s Seat  

The ignition hums—a low, unsteady prayer—  
her small hands grip the wheel, white-knuckled, bare.  

I watch the rearview: her breath a silver cloud,  
my own reflection blurred by sudden air.  

She stalls at the stop sign, trembling, then restarts—  
the engine coughs like something learning care.  

Her foot hovers above the clutch, suspended—  
a lifetime held between two pedals, there.  

We pass the oak where I once scraped my first fender,  
its bark still scored with memory’s old scar.  

She shifts too late; the car lurches forward—  
and in that lurch, I feel my father near.  

No lesson lasts beyond the open road—  
only this: love, unspoken, steering clear.

title: short lyric poem|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
Spring Blossom  
Petals drift like snowfall, light—  
a breath of pink and white.  
Bees hum in the warming hush,  
buds swell, tight fists uncurling.  
The earth exhales: damp, sweet, new.  

Summer Fruit  
Green globes swell, then blush—  
amber, ruby, gold.  
Leaves thick as shade, heavy with sun,  
branches bowing under weight and heat.  
A wasp drowses on split skin, sweet and sharp.  

Autumn Harvest  
Ladders lean. Baskets fill.  
Wind combs the thinning boughs—  
apples thud, brown-soft, into hay.  
Geese etch the grey sky;  
the orchard sheds its bright coat, bare and wise.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
Coffee at Dawn

In twilight's hush, the world still draped in sleep,
I rise to meet the silent, breaking day,
The kitchen light a solitary keep,
Where shadows softly wane and fade away.
The grinder hums its low and steady tune,
As fragrant beans their rich aroma yield,
A symphony beneath the waning moon,
That stirs the quiet with its warmth and shield.

The kettle's hiss, the pour, the gentle steam,
Each step a rite, a sacred, cherished dance,
And as I sip, a calm and peaceful dream
Envelops me, a sweet, serene expanse.
Thus fortified, I greet the sun's first ray,
With coffee's strength, I face the break of day.

title: ghazal|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The foghorn’s groan—like a bassoon left in rain—  
shudders the salt-crusted pane.  

My coffee’s gone cold, thick with grounds like silt,  
and the logbook’s last page holds only my name.  

I counted the bolts on the lantern’s brass ring:  
forty-three. Not forty-two. Not forty-four.  

The gulls don’t circle—they *stall*, wings locked,  
then drop like stones into the churning shore.  

My thermos leaks a slow amber bead—  
not honey, not rust, but old turpentine.  

The Fresnel lens throws fractured light:  
a shattered honeycomb, a broken spine.  

I folded my uniform—sleeves first—  
laid it flat as a pressed fern on the cot.  

The tide’s not rising. It’s *unspooling*,  
a gray thread pulled from the cliff’s raw throat.  

At 3:17 a.m., the bulb hummed once—  
then went out clean, like a held breath released.  

No storm. No wreck. Just the keeper’s hand  
still warm on the switch, still un-erased.

title: ode|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
November 12th, 2023  
Lake Minnetonka, west shore—  
the ice isn’t *solid* yet, just a skin,  
a milky scum where the reeds still poke through,  
brown and brittle as old matchsticks.  

I stood there in my dad’s wool cap,  
the one with the frayed brim and the moth hole  
just above the left ear—  
he died last March, but the smell of lanolin and pipe smoke  
still clings to the lining.  

Then: a ragged V, low,  
not soaring, *skimming*,  
wings beating like fists against the cold air—  
twenty-seven? thirty-two? I counted twice, lost at twenty-one.  
Their cries weren’t clean or noble—  
more like rusty hinges,  
a guttural *kronk-kronk* that snagged on the wind,  
then a softer, wetter *huh-huh-huh* from the stragglers.  

One bird dipped, wingtip brushing the ice-skin—  
a crack, thin as a hairline fracture,  
spreading maybe six inches before stopping.  
No drama. No metaphor. Just water breathing under glass.  

They passed over the dead cattails,  
over the half-submerged canoe I haven’t dragged ashore since October,  
its hull crusted with grey ice and a single frozen leaf,  
maple, curled tight as a fist.  

I didn’t think about migration routes or climate change or even my mother’s voice on the phone yesterday,  
saying *you sound tired, honey*.  
I just watched the V shrink,  
heard the kronking fade into the hollow hum  
of the power lines strung low across the marsh,  
and pulled my collar up,  
because the wind had shifted,  
and suddenly it was colder.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
In hidden corridors, the clatter sings,
Where stainless steel and laughter intertwine,
A bride in white, a groom with joyous grins,
Their love a feast for eyes, not just for wine.

Beyond the swinging doors, where guests are dressed
In finery that glitters, soft and bright,
We toil in shadows, chefs and waiters blessed
With tales of rings and vows recited right.

The kitchen's heat, a second sun, beats down,
As we prepare each dish with care, with pride.
In every plate, a story is crowned,
Of two hearts joined, their journey now allied.

Though unseen, our hands have played a part,
In crafting scenes of love, a work of art.

title: sequence of haiku|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
Midnight Threshold  
Clock hands freeze—  
a hollow in the chest where sleep should pool.  
Fridge hums low, awake.  

The Blue Hour  
Door opens: cold light spills like liquid glass.  
Empty shelves echo.  
The hum deepens—bone-deep, unrelenting.  

Dawn’s Faint Static  
First gray bleeds through curtains.  
Fridge sighs, its drone softening—  
still humming, still waiting.

title: ballad in quatrains|an abandoned railway station
text:
Whispers at Blackwood Junction

The iron tracks lie cold and bare,  
Where wild vines twist and choke the air;  
The signal arm hangs slack and low—  
No whistle cries, no engines go.  

The ticket booth’s cracked glass reflects  
A sky where weary starlings rest;  
Its ink-stained counter, warped and thin,  
Still holds the ghost of where I’ve been.  

The waiting room with peeling paint  
Holds echoes of a vanished saint—  
A child’s lost glove upon the floor,  
A name half-scraped from off the door.  

The platform’s edge, all rust and stone,  
Watches the wind move soft and lone;  
And though no train will ever call,  
The rails still dream—and wait—and fall.

title: elegy|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
In the shallow cradle of the sea,  
where water whispers to stone,  
hermit crabs scuttle like old men,  
carrying their worlds on their backs.

Here, the tide pools are quiet graves,  
etched with the salt of forgotten storms.  
Each shell a crypt, each shadowed crevice  
a sanctuary for the small and the slow.

The crabs, in borrowed armor,  
scour the edges of this liquid mirror,  
their eyes on stalks, twin periscopes  
searching for the next hollow home.

They trade shells like secrets,  
whispering through the brine,  
each move a dance of necessity,  
each retreat a step toward survival.

In the ebb, they are marionettes,  
pulled by invisible strings,  
tangled in the kelp’s embrace,  
while the gulls cry out above,  
witnesses to this silent ballet.

And when the tide returns,  
they vanish, swallowed by the deep,  
leaving only the empty husks,  
the discarded shells,  
like echoes of their fleeting presence.

title: ode|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
Ode to a Voice Across the Years  

The ring—a startled bird against the quiet,  
a tremor in the hollow of my palm.  
I fumble, breath caught like a thread too tight—  
and then: that voice, both stranger and a balm.  

Not changed, yet altered—rougher at the edges,  
warmed by miles I’d forgotten how to name,  
carrying echoes of our childhood ledges,  
the same low laugh that lit our shared small flame.  

No hello first—just “Remember how we’d climb  
the oak behind the shed? You always dropped  
the rope—I caught you, every single time.”  
My throat knots tight; the years go suddenly stopped.  

Static hums, a ghost between us, thin and thin—  
yet through it, clear as water over stone:  
the boy who stole my socks, who let me win  
at checkers just to keep me near his throne.  

We speak of mothers, fathers, roads we took,  
of silences we thought would never end—  
but here, now, in this fragile, humming book  
of sound, the broken is beginning to mend.  

The call ends soft. The line goes still. I hold  
the silent phone—and feel, at last, unalone.

title: poem in tercets|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Cemetery Leaves  

They drift—not fall—like sighs the earth exhales,  
a slow descent through slanting, silver light:  
crimson, ochre, gold that softly fails.  

Each name on stone grows fainter in the blight  
of rust and rain; the wind’s low, hollow tune  
stirs brittle wings above the quiet night.  

A maple key spins, lost beneath the moon,  
its tiny wing a spiral, frail and thin—  
like prayers unspooled, half-remembered, soon  

to crumble into dust where roots begin.  
No grave is cold while colour still takes flight:  
this hush is not an end—it is a kin.

title: pantoum|a jazz club in the rain
text:
Rainy Night Rhythms
In the heart of the city, rain taps on the roof,  
Soft whispers of jazz fill the night's quiet proof.  
Under dim lights, shadows dance with the beat,  
Voices mingle, in the warmth, no one wants to retreat.

 Shadows and Solos
Soft whispers of jazz fill the night's quiet proof,  
A saxophone wails, its cry a velvet truth.  
Voices mingle, in the warmth, no one wants to retreat,  
Laughter spills out, as secrets and stories meet.

 Closing Chords
A saxophone wails, its cry a velvet truth,  
In the heart of the city, rain taps on the roof.  
Laughter spills out, as secrets and stories meet,  
Under dim lights, shadows dance with the beat.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
Orchard’s Turning Year

When spring first stirs, the orchard wears a gown  
Of blushing pink and white—soft blossoms cling  
To slender boughs where hopeful breezes crown  
Each fragile branch with perfume, light, and wing.  
Then summer swells: green leaves grow thick and deep,  
And fruit hangs low in clusters, round and gold—  
Warm sun pours honeyed promises to keep,  
While drowsy bees in dappled shadows hold  
Their humming vigil. But the air grows thin,  
And autumn comes with russet, flame, and rust:  
The boughs bow low beneath the harvest’s grin,  
Then shed their jewels—crimson, amber, dust.  
At last, winter strips the branches bare—  
Yet roots remember spring, and wait with care.

title: pantoum|watching a parent grow old
text:
The coffee cup trembles—not the hand,  
but the ceramic’s thin blue glaze,  
a hairline crack where heat won’t stand.  
He counts pills into a Dixie cup’s haze.  

Not the hand, but the ceramic’s thin blue glaze—  
frost still clinging to the freezer door’s seal,  
he counts pills into a Dixie cup’s haze,  
then stares at the microwave’s dead, blank wheel.  

Frost still clinging to the freezer door’s seal,  
a half-eaten slice of apple pie, browned and dry,  
he stares at the microwave’s dead, blank wheel,  
while the garage door groans, stuck halfway high.  

A half-eaten slice of apple pie, browned and dry,  
his reading glasses fogged by steam from soup he won’t taste,  
while the garage door groans, stuck halfway high—  
the lawn mower’s cord, frayed, coiled like a snake’s waste.  

His reading glasses fogged by steam from soup he won’t taste,  
the TV remote buried in couch cushions, cold,  
the lawn mower’s cord, frayed, coiled like a snake’s waste—  
and his wristwatch, stopped at 3:17, unrolled.  

The TV remote buried in couch cushions, cold,  
the coffee cup trembles—not the hand,  
and his wristwatch, stopped at 3:17, unrolled.  
The ceramic’s thin blue glaze.

title: ode|the night shift at a diner
text:
Ode to the Night Shift at a Diner

In twilight's embrace, where the city lights gleam,
A diner stands, in the streetlamp's beam.
The night shift calls, with a siren so sweet,
To the guardians of the late-night eat.

When the world sleeps, and dreams take flight,
They flip the pancakes, till morning light.
Eggs over easy, or sunny-side up,
In the kitchen's warmth, they never give up.

Coffee brews, rich and dark as the sky,
Served with smiles, no matter how high
The stack of orders, or long the night,
Their spirits shine, oh so bright.

Through the door, drifters, workers, and more,
Seeking solace, on this midnight shore.
With a nod, a wink, and a gentle cheer,
They're served with care, year after year.

In the quiet hours, stories are shared,
Of lives lived fully, though sometimes scared.
The night crew listens, with hearts wide open,
In this little haven, no one is broken.

So here's to them, the unsung heroes,
Who keep the diner aglow, like halos.
Underneath the stars, in the heart of the night,
They make the world feel a little more right.

title: villanelle|a jazz club in the rain
text:
Rain hammers the awning—tin roof drumming,  
a bassline gone sour in the alley’s damp throat.  
Inside, the sax coughs smoke and a low, tired humming.  

Lena’s at the bar, stirring her third gin,  
her left heel clicking time against the stool’s worn oak.  
Rain hammers the awning—tin roof drumming.  

The piano’s out of tune; last night’s spilled beer left a stain  
on middle C, still sticky under Hank’s thick thumb.  
Inside, the sax coughs smoke and a low, tired humming.  

I know the crack in the brick behind the stage—  
saw it widen last Tuesday, after the double set.  
Rain hammers the awning—tin roof drumming.  

Marlon’s tie’s loosened, one button undone,  
his cufflink—a tiny brass sax—half-buried in sweat.  
Inside, the sax coughs smoke and a low, tired humming.  

That kid from ’98 came back tonight—  
same gap-toothed grin, same nervous laugh, same old coat.  
Rain hammers the awning—tin roof drumming.  
Inside, the sax coughs smoke and a low, tired humming.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
I. The Descent  
Upon the stair, a breathless, jostling press,  
Where weary souls in hurried silence tread;  
The turnstile’s click—a cold, metallic yes—  
As hope and haste are measured out in dread.  
Each face a mask of sleepless, softened strain,  
Eyes fixed on phones or floors, not one another;  
The air grows thick with damp wool, coffee, rain,  
And time contracts beneath the vaulted mother  
Of brick and steel. A siren wails afar—  
We pause, then plunge like fish into the deep:  
No word is spoken, yet we all know where  
The iron serpent waits to coil and leap.  
So down we go—not lost, but held in thrall,  
Beneath the city’s pulse, both mute and tall.  

II. The Carriage  
The doors hiss shut—a gasp, a shudder, tight—  
Then lurching forward, metal groans and sways.  
Shoulders brush shoulders in the yellow light,  
A forest pressed in hurried, human ways.  
A toddler clings, a backpack scrapes a knee,  
An old man grips the strap with trembling hold;  
A student’s earbuds leak a melody,  
While someone’s lunch gives off a scent too bold.  
No eye meets eye—yet glances flicker, brief,  
Like startled birds that dare not alight long;  
We share the sway, the pause, the shared relief  
When brakes release us from the crush and throng.  
This moving cage, though cramped and stark and loud,  
Holds kinship unconfessed within its crowd.  

III. The Ascent  
At last—the chime, the sigh, the parting tide,  
As bodies shift toward doors that gape and gleam.  
One step, two steps—then daylight, wide and wide—  
We surface, changed, yet bound by common dream.  
No farewells pass; no names are ever known;  
Yet something softens in the lifted gaze—  
A nod, a smile, a glance that’s briefly shown  
Before the street reclaims its separate ways.  
We walk apart, refreshed by shared constraint,  
Carrying quiet strength from close-held space;  
The city breathes, and we, though bruised, remain  
Both strangers and companions in this place.  
For every ride, though brief, has left its trace:  
A pulse aligned, a moment, shared, embraced.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
Title: Silent Reels and Unspoken Bonds

Upon the morn, with mist still in the air,
My silent uncle by the river's side,
We cast our lines, where waters gently pair
With whispers of the tide.

No words between us fill the quiet space,
Yet much is shared beneath the sun's soft gaze.
In every nod, a fond familiar grace,
And in his eyes, old memories ablaze.

The fish, they bite, or pass the bait along,
Our patience like the stones we stand upon.
Each catch, a dance of skill, without a song,
A silent symphony at dawn.

Though tongues be still, our hearts converse with ease,
In tranquil bonds that time nor talk can cease.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
The lot’s asphalt still breathes heat—thin, gray steam  
rising where tire-tracks melt the first thin lace  
of snow. A gurney’s wheel, half-buried, gleams  
like a dropped spoon in this pale, shifting space.  

No hush. A siren stitches through the air,  
then stops—leaving the hum of the ER door,  
its automatic sigh, its yellow glare  
spilling salt-crystal grit across the floor.  

A nurse leans on her car, smokes one slow drag,  
watching flakes snag in her eyelash fringe—  
not angels, not ermine, just static, vague,  
each one a tiny, flawed, collapsing hinge.  

Her coffee cup steams. The snow keeps falling,  
not blessing, not warning—just doing its calling.

title: villanelle|time and memory
text:
Time and Memory  

The clock’s thin hands dissect the light,  
While memory slips like sand through glass—  
A vanished face, a fading sight.  

I trace the contours of the night  
Where echoes gather, soft and vast;  
The clock’s thin hands dissect the light.  

Old photographs grow pale and white,  
Their edges curling as time passes—  
A vanished face, a fading sight.  

The voice I loved has lost its height,  
Its timbre blurred, its meaning cast  
The clock’s thin hands dissect the light.  

I call your name into the blight  
Of silence—no reply, no last  
A vanished face, a fading sight.  

What lingers is not wrong or right,  
But warmth that time could never mass—  
The clock’s thin hands dissect the light,  
A vanished face, a fading sight.

title: blank verse meditation|learning a second language as an adult
text:
In the quiet of my kitchen, under the hum of the old fridge,
I wrestle with verbs, like a child trying to tie their shoes,
Fingers fumbling over sounds that slip and slide,
A dance of the tongue, clumsy, ungraceful.

My dictionary, worn at the edges, lies open,
A map of a land I've yet to fully explore,
Each word a city, each phrase a winding road.
The coffee grows cold as I trace these paths,
Muttering to myself, a stranger in this new world.

Outside, the rain taps a steady beat on the window,
A rhythm I try to mimic, but it eludes me,
Like the laughter of friends in a café, fluid and warm,
While I stumble, a tourist, lost in translation.

Some days, it feels like swimming upstream,
Against a current of unfamiliar tides,
Other days, a breakthrough, a moment of clarity,
When the words flow, and I am almost fluent.

But always, there is the gap, the space between
What I know and what I yearn to express,
A chasm I bridge with fragments, with gestures,
With the hope that one day, I'll find my footing.

title: dramatic monologue|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
The Ring  

It begins—not with a voice, but with the *hush*  
before the storm: the refrigerator’s low hum  
cutting out. The kettle’s whistle, frozen mid-breath.  
My hand, hovering over the mug—steam curling, then still—  
as the phone *shivers* on the oak counter,  
a black beetle trembling in the afternoon light.  

I don’t recognize the number.  
Just six digits blinking like cold stars.  
I answer anyway. Not hope—no, not yet—  
but the old, dumb muscle of answering  
what rings in the hollow of a house too quiet.  

Then—*a breath*. Not mine.  
A pause thick as river silt.  
And then: *“Lena?”*  
Not “Lena?”—but *Lena?*,  
the way he used to say it when we were ten,  
kneeling in the gravel driveway,  
splitting a stolen peach between us,  
juice running down our wrists like liquid gold.  

My throat closes. Not with tears—not yet—  
but with the sudden, shocking weight  
of a name spoken *exactly right*:  
the slight lift at the end, the soft *a* like an open door,  
the ghost of our mother’s lilt,  
the cadence I haven’t heard in twenty-three years,  
twenty-three winters, twenty-three autumns  
where I kept his birthday in my pocket like a smooth, cold stone.  

He says, *“I’m outside.”*  
I look up—past the rain-streaked window,  
past the rusted swing set, past the oak where we carved our initials—  
and there he is.  
Not a man I remember, but a man *made* of memory:  
taller, thinner, hair gone salt-and-ash,  
but the same crooked shadow under his left eye,  
the same hesitant tilt of the head  
when he’s about to tell a truth that costs him.  
He holds a paper cup—coffee, probably—  
steam rising, vanishing, rising again.  

I don’t move.  
The phone stays pressed to my ear.  
His voice is smaller now, frayed at the edges:  
*“I didn’t know if you’d pick up.  
Or if you’d want to.”*  

Outside, a sparrow lands on the fence rail.  
Tilts its head. Watches.  
The cup in his hand trembles—just once—  
and a single drop falls, dark and slow,  
onto the cracked concrete.  

I don’t speak.  
I let the silence hold us both:  
the brother who vanished into the static of a bad connection,  
the sister who kept his voice alive in her bones,  
and this thin, bright wire humming between us—  
alive, unbroken,  
terrible as a live wire,  
beautiful as the first note after years of silence.  

The sparrow flies.  
The steam rises.  
The drop dries.  
I breathe.  
And the phone, still warm against my skin,  
holds the shape of his name—  
not spoken, not released—  
but *held*,  
like breath before the plunge,  
like light before the lens focuses,  
like the exact, unbearable second  
before the world rewrites itself.

title: prose poem|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
Sunday Stillness

Sunlight slants through the high, dusty windows—thin gold blades slicing the hush. The air smells of aging paper, leather bindings softened by decades, and the faint, sweet ghost of pipe tobacco long since exhaled into memory. Shelves rise like silent sentinels, their spines a muted alphabet of green, burgundy, navy, and faded gold—titles half-remembered, authors half-known, stories waiting not to be found but to be *recognized*. A single patron sits at the oak reading table, head bent, fingers tracing lines as if reading Braille on the page; her breath is the only rhythm beside the slow, steady *tick* of the brass clock above the circulation desk—its hands frozen at 3:47, though it keeps perfect time. Somewhere deep in the stacks, a floorboard sighs. A pigeon alights on the ledge outside, tilts its head, peers in—not at the books, but at the quiet itself, as if astonished that such density of thought could hold so much silence. Even the dust motes hang suspended, turning lazily in the light, not falling, not rising—just *being*, like every unwritten sentence, every unasked question, every life paused between covers. This is not absence. It is presence, thick and tender, held in trust. The library does not sleep on Sunday. It breathes.

title: blank verse meditation|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Under the stadium lights, moths orbit,
their shadows flicker like old film reels
on the field’s green canvas. The air hums
with a low buzz, not just the crowd's roar
but the electric pulse of night itself.

A player crouches, his helmet a mirror
to the moon, reflecting a ghostly face—
not his own, but something older, wilder.
His breath fogs in the chill, a dragon’s sigh
in the arena of high school dreams.

The ball is a heart, thudding, passed
from hand to hard, each beat a story:
a mother’s late shift, a father’s silence,
the quiet hope that pulses through veins
like the town’s hidden river, unseen, deep.

On the sidelines, cheerleaders stretch,
their voices sharp as the crack of a whip,
each chant a small rebellion, a whispered
promise of escape. Their eyes, though, linger
on the distant hills, where the dark swallows
everything, even the stars.

The coach paces, a lion in a cage,
his clipboard a shield, his words a mantra
that no one truly hears. His mind drifts
to the empty house, the cold dinner,
the silent phone, and he wonders if
victory can fill those hollow spaces.

In the stands, an old man with gnarled hands
clutches a faded jersey, the number
blurred by time. He remembers when
he was the hero, the town’s pride, now
just another shadow in the bleachers,
waiting for the final whistle, the end
of another Friday, another year,
another chapter in the endless book
of this small town, under the watchful
eyes of the unblinking stars.

title: elegy|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
Elegy for the Unattended Garden  

The gate hangs loose on rusted hinges,  
A sigh of iron, slow and thin.  
No hand turns soil where mint still lingers—  
Its stems grow wild, its roots wear thin.  

Roses, unpruned, arch in tangled grace,  
Petals like ash on dampened stone.  
The fountain’s throat is choked with lace  
Of moss and time’s unyielding tone.  

Clematis climbs the empty arbor, blind,  
Its violet stars no longer named.  
The scarecrow slumps—his burlap mind  
Unstitched, his straw by wind unclaimed.  

Bees hum low above the thistle’s crown,  
A hymn without a hearer’s ear.  
The sundial casts no telling down—  
Just shadow, drifting, year on year.  

And yet—beneath the cracked brick path,  
Where nettles kiss the lavender’s last breath—  
Something persists: not grief, but aftermath—  
A quiet pulse that outlives death.

title: ghazal|the sound of a train at night
text:
The 11:47 from Albany groans past my window—  
not a whistle, but that low, wet rattle in the couplers.  

I’m still in yesterday’s socks, one heel frayed,  
listening to the steel sigh like my father’s old Buick.  

That squeal on the curve near the cemetery gate?  
Yeah—that’s the same rail where Mrs. Gable’s cat got flattened.  

My coffee’s gone cold, thick as tar at the bottom of the mug,  
and the light above the stove flickers, then steadies.  

I count the cars: grain hopper, boxcar with peeling red paint,  
then three empties—windows all boarded up tight.  

Sometimes I wave, just to see if anyone’s looking back—  
but the conductor’s cab’s dark, and the glass is too grimy.  

Last week it carried a coffin crate, pine-scented and nailed shut,  
and the next morning, rain washed the soot off my sill.  

I don’t know why I keep the blinds cracked an inch.  
I just do. Like breathing. Like forgetting to lock the door.

title: elegy|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
In the heart where gears once spun, a silence deep,
The factory's breath now stilled, in shadows steep.
Brick walls, like ancient guards, stand watch alone,
Over streets that whisper tales of what was known.

Rusted gates, no longer clanking to the beat,
Of hurried feet, or laughter, or the heat
Of furnaces that roared beneath the sky,
Now echo with the soft sighs of goodbye.

Windows, eyes to a world long since passed,
Gaze out over an emptiness vast.
No more the clang of metal on metal sound,
Just the wind, as it wanders, without bound.

Children’s chalk drawings fade from cracked sidewalks,
Memories etched, by hands small, and talks
Of futures bright, in dreams once tightly held,
Now scattered like leaves, by stories untold.

Elderly sit, on porches worn by time,
Their faces maps of joy and lines of prime,
When life here thrived, and every home had light,
And hope was not just a word, but a sight.

Night falls, and stars peek through the smoky haze,
A reminder of days when dreams were ablaze.
Yet, in this quiet, there's a gentle peace,
As if the town itself, has found release.

For though the machines have ceased their endless dance,
And jobs, like autumn leaves, have lost their chance,
There lingers still, within these hollowed halls,
A spirit unbroken, answering calls.

To rise again, perhaps, in different guise,
Or simply rest, beneath the wide, wise skies.
This factory town, in its final pose,
Whispers softly, "Let go, let grow."

title: prose poem|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
The First Grind  
The grinder hums—a low, insistent bee trapped in ceramic. Dark beans shatter into dust that smells like burnt sugar and distant earth. My fingers are still half-asleep, fumbling the scoop, but the ritual holds: coarse for the French press, fine for the pour-over, precise as prayer. Outside, the sky is the color of weak tea, and the house breathes in silence—no footsteps, no sighs, no clink of spoons yet. Just this: the scent rising, sharp and green and ancient, as if waking the world before the world knows it’s been called.

The Bloom  
Water just off the boil hits the grounds—first a swell, then a slow, dark exhale. Bubbles rise like tiny planets forming. Steam curls, thin and silver, carrying the heart of the bean: walnut, cedar, a whisper of cherry left to ferment in the sun. I watch the bloom collapse into liquid gravity, rich and opaque. The kettle cools on the stove. A bird calls once—tentative, unpracticed. The cup waits, empty and warm in my palms, holding only the shape of what’s coming.

The First Sip  
Heat first, then bitterness—not harsh, but deep, like soil after rain. Then sweetness unfolds, slow and surprising, like light finding the corner of the room. My shoulders drop. My breath steadies. The world hasn’t stirred, but I am no longer waiting for it—I am already inside the day, anchored by this small, steaming truth. The cup is half-empty before I remember to taste the air again: cool, quiet, full of unlived hours. Dawn isn’t breaking. It’s brewing. And I am here, awake, holding warmth in both hands.

title: free verse poem|a small-town Friday football game
text:
The bleachers groan—not wood, but rusted steel  
buckling under the weight of folded lawn chairs,  
a toddler’s sippy cup leaking blue Gatorade  
onto a cracked vinyl seat.  

Coach’s whistle isn’t shrill—it’s a snapped rubber band  
against his thumbnail, then silence thick as the smell  
of hot asphalt and someone’s burnt popcorn  
spilling from a paper bag held too long in a fist.  

Quarterback’s helmet visor fogs—not from breath,  
but from the condensation of his own pulse,  
a slow bead tracing the curve where his temple meets plastic.  

A girl in the third row chews gum with her mouth open,  
blows a bubble that doesn’t pop—just trembles,  
translucent, catching the floodlights like a lens  
focusing light on the scuffed white stripe  
where the kicker plants his left cleat:  
not grass, but packed dirt, gravel, and one stubborn dandelion  
pushing through the chalk line like a green question mark.  

The band plays “Seven Nation Army”—  
not the anthem, not the fight song—  
just the bassline thumping through the bleachers’ ribs,  
vibrating the soda can someone left behind,  
its tab loose, clicking softly against the aluminum  
like a tiny, indifferent metronome.  

When the final whistle blows, no one cheers right away.  
Just the hollow *thunk* of shoulder pads hitting the turf,  
a coach wiping his nose with the sleeve of a sweat-stiffened shirt,  
and the distant, rhythmic *shush-shush-shush*  
of the custodian’s broom on the track—  
sweeping up nothing but dust, glitter, and a single earbud,  
still pulsing faintly, still warm.

title: poem in tercets|moving out of a childhood home
text:
Leaving the Nest

In rooms where laughter once did play,  
Now echoes softly, day by day.  
Each corner holds a memory's sway.

Beneath the window, moonbeams creep,  
I pack my dreams, so light, so deep.  
A heart that yearns to sail the steep.

The walls, they whisper of the past,  
Of secrets kept and friendships cast.  
Yet time, it moves, too swift, too fast.

With every box, a chapter ends,  
New paths await, with twists and bends.  
My childhood home, on you, I send...

A final glance, a silent vow,  
To cherish all, here and now.  
For in my heart, your spirit plows.

title: pantoum|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
The 7:15 local smells of damp wool and burnt coffee,  
a man’s earbuds leak bass I feel in my molars,  
my left knee pressed to the pole, cold and slick—  
someone’s grocery bag swings, bruising my calf.  

A man’s earbuds leak bass I feel in my molars,  
his jacket’s frayed at the cuff, thumb hooked in a pocket.  
Someone’s grocery bag swings, bruising my calf—  
I count tiles on the ceiling: three cracked, one missing.  

His jacket’s frayed at the cuff, thumb hooked in a pocket,  
a toddler wails, then stops, stares at my chipped nail polish.  
I count tiles on the ceiling: three cracked, one missing—  
the train lurches; a woman’s tote spills loose mints.  

A toddler wails, then stops, stares at my chipped nail polish,  
her mother hums off-key, breath smelling faintly of toast.  
The train lurches; a woman’s tote spills loose mints—  
I don’t bend. My spine remembers yesterday’s rain.  

Her mother hums off-key, breath smelling faintly of toast,  
and the doors hiss open onto steam and a shout I can’t place.  
I don’t bend. My spine remembers yesterday’s rain.  
My stop’s coming. I shift my weight. The light flickers.

title: poem in tercets|an old piano left on the curb
text:
Curb Piano  

Its lid hangs open like a slack jaw,  
yellowed keys—ivory ghosts, chipped and thin—  
still hold the shape of vanished hands’ raw law.  

Rain has blurred the maker’s brass plate, dim,  
a smudge of “Steinway & Sons” half-drowned in grime;  
one leg leans, splintered, on a broken limb.  

A sparrow hops across the bass clef’s rhyme,  
pecks at dust where middle C once sang—  
a hollow thud replies, no note, no time.  

The streetlight bleeds its sodium stain  
on strings gone slack as gutted harp-strings, rust  
coiling like old grief down the soundboard’s grain.  

No one stops. A dog sniffs, then turns to trust  
the scent of garbage bags. The wind slips in,  
stirs moth-wing felt—and something almost must  

rise: a chord unsounded, deep within  
the wood’s slow sigh, the curb’s cold, waiting stone—  
a hymn the city left, but won’t let in.

title: blank verse meditation|an abandoned railway station
text:
Echoes of Departure

In the stillness, where once a throng did move,
The old station stands, silent as a tomb.
Rails stretch out like arms, embracing none,
Their iron cold, untouched by sun or moon.
Windows stare, blind and dusty, at the sky,
As if in search for trains that never come.

Whispers of the Past

Ghosts of travelers linger in the air,
Soft murmurs caught within the crumbling walls.
A ticket booth, now home to spiders' webs,
Holds echoes of hurried feet and farewells said.
Bench seats bear the weight of absent souls,
Waiting still, though time has moved ahead.

Nature's Quiet Reclaim

Vines creep over tracks, their slow advance
Unhindered by the schedules they replace.
Wildflowers bloom through cracks in concrete floors,
Painting life upon this canvas, worn and bare.
Birds nest where the stationmaster stood,
And nature whispers softly, "I am here."

title: short lyric poem|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
Tide Pool Alchemy

The tide recedes—a liquid sigh—  
leaving silver saucers, deep and shy.  
Each a world of glass and gleam:  
anemones bloom in slow, salt dream,  
limpets cling with ancient grace,  
and kelp fronds trace the water’s lace.  

Then—scuttle-scratch! A rustled sound:  
a hermit crab on stony ground.  
His borrowed shell, a spiraled keep,  
holds more than flesh—it holds the deep:  
the ghost of waves, the moon’s soft call,  
the weight of ocean, small yet tall.  

He tests the edge where light and brine entwine—  
a tenant of the ebb’s design.  
No king, no slave—just pulse, just shell,  
a living question, brief and well:  
*What home is true when tides command?*  
He carries sea within his hand.

title: free verse poem|learning a second language as an adult
text:
The Late Bloomer’s Tongue  

First, the tongue feels foreign—  
a stone lodged beneath the teeth,  
heavy with unfamiliar contours.  
You press it against the roof of your mouth  
and hear only silence, or worse:  
a clumsy echo that cracks like dry clay.  

Grammar charts bloom like thorny vines—  
conjugations twist, genders resist naming,  
prepositions hover like startled birds  
refusing to land where logic says they should.  

You memorize “bonjour” but forget it mid-breath,  
stumble over “ser” and “estar” as if choosing between ghosts,  
mispronounce “ración” so the cashier smiles gently—  
not unkindly, but with the quiet patience  
reserved for someone coaxing a shy animal from the dark.  

There are days the language lives only in your head—  
a museum of perfect verbs behind glass,  
untouchable, unlived.  
Then, one Tuesday, you order coffee—  
no notes, no rehearsal—  
and the words spill warm and whole,  
and the barista says “¡Qué bien!”  
and something inside you unclenches, just once.  

It is not fluency you gather, but fragments:  
a phrase that fits like a key turned in a long-rusted lock,  
a joke that lands—not perfectly, but *there*,  
a silence you finally recognize as shared, not empty.  

You learn the language not by erasing your first,  
but by letting it hum beneath the new—  
a bassline beneath an uncertain melody.  
Your accent is not a flaw. It is a borderland.  
A place where two worlds kneel,  
not to merge, but to meet—  
knee to knee,  
breath to breath,  
learning how to listen  
in the beautiful, broken space between.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
Under the moon’s pale gaze, a canvas wide,
Stretched over tents that huddle in the night,
A child with eyes like stars, and dreams denied,
Draws constellations on the canvas tight.

The air is thick with whispers, prayers, and smoke,
From fires where elders share their silent fears.
A mother hums a lullaby, her cloak
Enfolding shadows, drying little tears.

The moon, a witness to this quiet scene,
Casts silver light upon each weary face,
And though it shines so bright, so serene,
It cannot mend the wounds time will not erase.

I see my own lost kin in every line,
Their stories etched in light, forever mine.

title: pantoum|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
First Snow in the Hospital Parking Lot  

The sky unspools its hush of ash and lead,  
a slow descent—soft, silent, unafraid.  
Gray light pools in the cracks where oil has bled,  
and tire tracks hold the cold like shallow graves.  

A slow descent—soft, silent, unafraid—  
snowflakes alight on windshields, thin and frail.  
And tire tracks hold the cold like shallow graves,  
while IV bags sway in rooms above the gale.  

Snowflakes alight on windshields, thin and frail,  
each one a breath held, trembling, then released.  
While IV bags sway in rooms above the gale,  
a mother counts the seconds—unrehearsed, unceasing.  

Each one a breath held, trembling, then released,  
the lot exhales—a mist of salt and steel.  
A mother counts the seconds—unrehearsed, unceasing—  
and somewhere, under snow, a heart begins to heal.

title: dramatic monologue|teenage summer jobs
text:
1. The Ice Cream Scoop  
I wear the paper hat like a crown of wilted lettuce,  
scoop swirls into cones while the register hums its tired hymn.  
Mrs. Gable’s grandkids demand “rainbow sprinkles—*extra*,”  
and I smile, my wrist aching, my hair stuck to my neck with heat.  
When the freezer door sighs open, I breathe deep—  
cold air sharp as apology—  
but the moment I step back out,  
the sun pins me down again,  
and all I am is sugar, sweat, and the ghost of vanilla.  

2. The Lawnmower’s Grumble  
This machine doesn’t obey—it *negotiates*:  
stutter, stall, spit grass clippings like green curses.  
I push it up Mr. Finch’s hill, shirt soaked through,  
ears ringing from the roar that drowns my own thoughts.  
He watches from his porch swing, sipping lemonade,  
while I dodge dandelions and dog leashes,  
wondering if freedom tastes like gasoline and cut grass,  
or if it’s just the quiet *after*,  
when the engine dies,  
and my arms remember how to hold still.  

3. The Closing Shift  
Keys jingle in my palm—cold, heavy, real.  
I lock the café door, flip the sign,  
wipe the counter one last time though it’s already clean.  
The espresso machine exhales steam like a tired god.  
My name tag reads *JORDAN — SMILE!*,  
but tonight I leave it on the hook,  
let the plastic curl at the edges,  
let the ink fade in the dark.  
Tomorrow I’ll be someone else again—  
but for now, walking home under streetlights waking up,  
I am just bones and breath,  
and the slow, sweet weight of having earned the night.

title: ballad in quatrains|time and memory
text:
Title: Echoes of Yesteryears

In the halls where whispers dwell, time's soft tread,
Memories like shadows, by moonlight spread.
Each moment a ghost that lingers and fades,
In the quiet corners, in the silent glades.

The clock ticks on, with steady, solemn gait,
Through corridors of years, through light and fate.
A keepsake here, a faded photograph there,
Holding the laughter, holding the despair.

We chase the sun, from dawn till evening's sigh,
Gathering moments as they flutter by.
Yet, in our hands, they turn to mist and air,
Leaving but echoes, leaving but a stare.

So let us cherish, while we may, this day,
For time, like water, will not stay.
In hearts and minds, the past shall find its way,
In the dance of memories, forever sway.

title: ode|the ocean during a storm
text:
Ode to the Storm-Sea  

Not a beast, not a god—  
just pressure dropping like a dropped plate,  
and the water’s sudden *unzipping*:  
a seam torn open where the horizon used to hold.  

The waves don’t rise—they *shatter upward*,  
glass shards of green-black light,  
each crest collapsing into its own cold breath,  
spitting salt that stings like crushed battery acid.  

That slick, oil-sheen purple on the troughs?  
Not iridescence—*rotting kelp*,  
pulped and fermenting under the wind’s thumb.  
And the gulls? Not crying—  
they’re *tacking sideways*, wings locked,  
beaks shut tight as zippers on a wet coat.  

The shore isn’t waiting.  
It’s *grinding*:  
granite teeth chewing basalt,  
sand hissing like hot griddles under rain.  
Even the lighthouse beam doesn’t pierce—  
it *drowns*, thick as congealed broth,  
swallowed before it clears the cliff’s raw edge.  

This isn’t rage.  
It’s physics unmoored:  
the deep’s cold breath rising,  
the air’s thin lungs heaving,  
and the water—always the water—  
not remembering its name,  
just *moving*,  
heavy, indifferent,  
full of drowned starlight  
and the slow, wet click  
of barnacles  
tightening.

title: pantoum|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
The espresso machine hisses, low and mean,  
while I scrape dried frosting off the cake stand—  
a smear of buttercream, pale as a bruise,  
and three stray rose petals stuck to the rim.  

While I scrape dried frosting off the cake stand,  
the bride’s cousin leans in, breath smelling of gin,  
and three stray rose petals stuck to the rim  
float in the sink like drowned moths, wings still whole.  

The bride’s cousin leans in, breath smelling of gin,  
says, “My sister’s dress got caught on the chandelier,”  
and float in the sink like drowned moths, wings still whole—  
I nod, wipe my hands on a towel stiff with sugar.  

Says, “My sister’s dress got caught on the chandelier,”  
and I remember the groom’s cufflink, bent sideways,  
I nod, wipe my hands on a towel stiff with sugar,  
then toss it into the bin where the wilted basil lies.  

And I remember the groom’s cufflink, bent sideways,  
found near the ice bucket, cold and tarnished,  
then toss it into the bin where the wilted basil lies—  
no one’s asked for it back. Not yet. Not ever, maybe.  

Found near the ice bucket, cold and tarnished,  
the dishwasher hums its tired, wet song,  
no one’s asked for it back. Not yet. Not ever, maybe.  
Outside, someone laughs. A real one. Sharp. Unplanned.

title: ode|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
In the heart of night, when stars hold sway,
A city bus at 2 a.m. makes its way.
Through streets that whisper under moonlit skies,
Its headlights cut through shadows, a silent surprise.

The engine hums a lullaby so low,
To the few souls who wander, in dreams they go.
Windows fogged with breaths of midnight air,
Each passenger a story, each one a rare.

An old man's eyes, reflecting distant lights,
His hands, like parchment, hold onto his nights.
A young girl lost in music, earbuds in,
Her world a secret, from the din and spin.

Outside, the city sleeps, a gentle beast,
Buildings stand as sentinels, in restful feast.
But on this bus, life pulses, soft and true,
A microcosm, in the vast, dark hue.

At every stop, the doors sigh open wide,
Letting in the night, and those who hide.
A couple boards, their laughter light and free,
Bringing warmth to seats, in company.

The driver, guardian of this moving space,
Guides them through the labyrinth, with steady pace.
His eyes, a map of roads, both known and new,
A quiet hero, in the hours so few.

And as the journey winds, through time and place,
This city bus, a sanctuary, finds its grace.
A vessel of stories, hopes, and fleeting dreams,
Carrying them softly, like a river's streams.

Till dawn breaks, and the world awakes anew,
The bus will carry on, till morning's dew.
In the heart of night, it weaves its spell,
A city bus at 2 a.m., where stories dwell.

title: villanelle|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
I. The Pool’s First Light  
The tide recedes, a silver, sighing trace,  
Leaving behind the world’s inverted glass—  
A liquid lens where time forgets its pace.  

Each basin holds a miniature sea-space:  
Anemones pulse, soft shadows softly pass,  
The tide recedes, a silver, sighing trace.  

A spiral shell lies still in brine’s embrace,  
Empty and waiting—hollow, cold, and vast.  
A liquid lens where time forgets its pace.  

No footfall stirs the algae’s emerald lace,  
Just salt-air hush and sunlight, thin and cast—  
The tide recedes, a silver, sighing trace.  

What waits beneath? What slow, small will replace  
This vacancy? No answer yet is asked.  
A liquid lens where time forgets its pace.  

II. The Shell-Seeker  
A pinch of legs, a twitch of cautious grace,  
He scuttles sideways where the water’s gone—  
A living question in that shallow place.  

His borrowed home, a whorled and weathered case,  
Too tight now, worn too thin beneath the dawn,  
A pinch of legs, a twitch of cautious grace.  

He pauses, probes the rim of empty space,  
Tests weight and curve with antennae withdrawn—  
A living question in that shallow place.  

One shell discarded, one embraced with haste,  
A fragile covenant, both brief and drawn—  
A pinch of legs, a twitch of cautious grace.  

No map he reads, no chart he can retrace,  
Just instinct’s pull, the tide’s unspoken spawn—  
A living question in that shallow place.  

III. The Turning Tide  
The water rises, hushed and slow and deep,  
Returning all it took—but not the same:  
New shells lie settled where old promises sleep.  

He clings now, sealed within his chosen keep,  
While kelp sways low and barnacles reclaim  
The water rises, hushed and slow and deep.  

The pool refills; the light begins to leap  
From wave to wave, a flickering, liquid flame—  
New shells lie settled where old promises sleep.  

No loss remains, no memory to keep,  
Just rhythm, shift, and quiet, constant claim—  
The water rises, hushed and slow and deep.  

The hermit moves—not forward, not to leap—  
But turns with tides, unchanged by change’s name.  
New shells lie settled where old promises sleep.

title: prose poem|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
The Silent Reel

Dawn bleeds thin and silver over the water’s skin, and he is already there—boots planted in damp silt, rod held like a prayer he never speaks. No greeting, no nod, just the quiet unspooling of line, the soft *shush* as it cuts air, then the faintest *plink* where it kisses the surface. I watch his hands: knuckles broad and sun-cracked, veins tracing maps beneath weathered skin, moving with the certainty of tides. He doesn’t teach; he simply *is*—a stillness that teaches by presence alone.

We sit on the splintered dock, knees drawn, elbows resting on thighs, rods angled just so—not too high, not too low—like two antennae tuned to the same mute frequency. The water holds its breath. A dragonfly hovers, iridescent and impatient. My line trembles once—just a whisper of current, or maybe a minnow’s passing thought—but his doesn’t stir. He watches the ripple fade, eyes the color of river stones, deep and unreflective.

Hours pool like slow amber. No words pass between us—not about the weather, not about school, not about the silence itself. His silence isn’t empty. It’s thick with the weight of cormorants diving, the sigh of reeds bending, the slow turn of a turtle’s head beneath the surface. It’s the space where language dissolves and something older takes hold—the pulse of gills, the drag of current, the patient geometry of waiting.

When the bobber dips—just once, decisively—he moves. Not fast, but absolute. A lift of the wrist, a steady pull, the rod arcing like a drawn bow. Silver flashes, thrashes, throws diamonds into the light. He guides it in with quiet authority, net dipping, scooping the wild, wet gleam. For a breath, he holds the fish aloft—gills flaring, tail shuddering against air—and I see his thumb, gentle, cradling the belly, before the release: a silver arc back into the hush, a widening ring, then nothing but water remembering.

He reels in, coiling the line with methodical loops. Packs the tackle. Wipes his hands on his trousers. Walks toward the truck without looking back. I follow. The silence walks with us—not heavy, not cold, but full, like the space between notes that makes the music true. It’s the only thing he ever gave me that didn’t need translation. It’s the first thing I learned to speak.

title: elegy|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
From here, it’s a sunset bleeding  
past its borders, spilling into night.  

Not the crackle of twigs underfoot,  
but a chorus of shattering glass—  
the forest exhales in shards.  

Smoke rises, not like fingers  
reaching for the sky, but as columns  
of ancient temples, crumbling,  
their gods long departed.  

Ashes drift down,  
not snowflakes, but the burnt  
edges of forgotten letters,  
messages from a world already gone.  

The fire is a painter, wild and bold,  
streaking the canvas with char,  
with strokes that erase  
and create in the same breath.  

In the distance, the trees are not candles,  
but the spines of old books,  
pages turning to embers,  
stories consumed by their own telling.  

And when the wind shifts,  
it carries not the scent of pine,  
but the acrid whisper of endings,  
a reminder that even the silent  
have a voice in the flames.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|drought on a family farm
text:
The Thirsting Soil  

Upon our fields where golden wheat once grew,  
Now cracked and bare the thirsty earth doth lie;  
No gentle rain descends to soothe the dew,  
Nor cloud doth weep to quench the ashen sky.  
The cattle low with hollow, aching throats,  
Their ribs like laths beneath thin, dusty hide;  
The well runs dry—no silver water floats,  
But dust and silence where cool streams did glide.  
My father’s hands, once calloused from the plough,  
Now trace the fissures with a trembling grace,  
As if to mend what drought hath stolen now—  
His hope, his harvest, time’s unyielding pace.  
Yet in this waste, though barren all appears,  
Love roots more deep than any vanished years.

title: elegy|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
Elegy for the Wedding, Seen from the Kitchen  

The chandelier’s cold fire trembles on polished silver—  
a hundred forks laid like fallen soldiers.  
We peel pears in silence, skin curling thin and gold,  
while upstairs, a violin bows its first, trembling note.  

Steam rises—not from the ovens, but from our necks,  
from the damp collar of Marco’s shirt,  
from the hollow behind Rosa’s ear where sweat gathers,  
like a tiny, unshed tear.  

The bride’s bouquet passes the service door—  
roses, peonies, sweet peas—  
a riot of perfume that makes Luis cough,  
then laugh, then wipe his nose on his sleeve.  
*Too much life,* he mutters, *all at once.*  

We hear the vows through the vent:  
*…for better, for worse…*  
A pause. A choked breath.  
Then the clink of crystal—not celebration, but correction—  
as someone lifts a glass too soon, too high,  
and the sound drops into our space like a dropped spoon.  

Later, the cake arrives—ivory tiers, sugar-dusted, absurdly tall—  
we carry it past the open door:  
a glimpse—her veil catching light,  
his hand trembling on her waist,  
their faces blurred by heat-haze from the pass-through.  
We do not look long.  
We have frosting under our nails,  
a burnt sugar smell clinging to our wrists,  
and the quiet certainty that love, like soufflé,  
rises only if no one watches it rise.  

At midnight, we scrape plates clean,  
stack chairs like gravestones,  
sweep petals from the floor—  
each one still soft, still holding the shape of a mouth  
that has just spoken *yes*.  

The last light flickers over stainless steel.  
We lock the walk-in.  
Outside, fireworks bloom—  
brief, loud, beautiful,  
and utterly indifferent  
to the way Rosa folds her apron,  
slowly,  
as if folding something she loved,  
but never held.

title: prose poem|hope after a long illness
text:
Whispers of Dawn

In the quiet, when night still clings to the edges of the world,  
A faint light breaks through, a whisper of dawn.  
It touches the tired eyelids, gently urging them open,  
To see beyond the shadows that have lingered so long.  
Hope, in its simplest form, is this first light,  
A promise that even the longest nights do end.

The Garden Awaits

Outside, a garden blooms, oblivious to the battles within,  
Petals unfurling in defiance of the darkness that once reigned.  
Each flower, a testament to resilience, stands tall and proud,  
Their colors a bold declaration: life persists, beauty abounds.  
Here, amidst the green and the gold, hope takes root,  
Growing stronger with each passing day, as the sun warms the soil and the soul.

Steps Toward the Horizon

With every step, the ground feels firmer underfoot,  
The horizon, once a distant dream, now calls with a clearer voice.  
The journey is not without its stumbles, but the view ahead  
Is filled with possibilities, each one a new chapter waiting to be written.  
Hope becomes the path, winding, sometimes steep,  
But always leading forward, toward a place where the heart can heal and soar.

title: pantoum|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Friday Night Lights

The bleachers groan with rust and pride,  
A patchwork quilt of flannel, foam, and cheers,  
As twilight melts to amber, deep and wide—  
The field waits hushed beneath the fading years.  

A patchwork quilt of flannel, foam, and cheers,  
Boys in pads like armor, tight and bright,  
The field waits hushed beneath the fading years,  
While fireflies blink above the floodlit height.  

Boys in pads like armor, tight and bright,  
Coach’s whistle cuts the thickening air,  
While fireflies blink above the floodlit height,  
And popcorn steam hangs light as whispered prayer.  

Coach’s whistle cuts the thickening air,  
A snap, a surge—a hopeful, thunderous run—  
And popcorn steam hangs light as whispered prayer,  
Then silence holds its breath… then scores are won.  

A snap, a surge—a hopeful, thunderous run,  
The band swells loud, brass burning through the night,  
Then silence holds its breath… then scores are won,  
And stars emerge, slow, steady, soft, and white.  

The band swells loud, brass burning through the night,  
The bleachers groan with rust and pride—  
And stars emerge, slow, steady, soft, and white—  
As twilight melts to amber, deep and wide.

title: spoken-word poem|the stars seen from a desert
text:
The desert doesn’t *hold* the stars—it *spills* them.  
Not like salt from a shaker, no—  
more like shattered headlight glass  
scattered across blacktop after a wreck nobody heard.  

That one there? Vega?  
It’s not a diamond. It’s a splinter of cold blue plastic  
stuck in the pad of my thumb  
when I was twelve, prying open a broken toy robot.  
Still stings when I tilt my wrist just right.  

And Orion’s Belt? Three rivets hammered crooked  
into rusted steel on the old water tower outside Yucca, Arizona—
