one’s loose. Wobbles. You can hear it hum  
if you press your ear to the metal at 2:17 a.m.,  
just before the coyotes stop barking  
and the wind forgets its own name.  

The Milky Way isn’t milk.  
It’s the residue left behind  
after scrubbing dried motor oil off a concrete floor  
with a stiff-bristled brush and too much ammonia—  
that faint, greasy, pearlescent smear  
that won’t lift, no matter how hard you scrub,  
no matter how much light you shine on it.  

And when the satellite passes?  
Not a silver thread, not a falling wish—  
it’s the slow, deliberate blink of a security camera  
mounted above a shuttered laundromat in Albuquerque,  
panning left, then pausing, then panning left again,  
recording nothing but heat-haze and dust devils  
dancing their dumb, three-second polka  
in the empty lot.  

I don’t ask the sky for meaning.  
I watch how the starlight lands  
on the cracked vinyl seat of my ’98 Corolla,  
how it pools in the shallow dent  
where my elbow rests,  
how it glints—not brightly, but *thickly*—  
off the dried coffee ring  
inside my chipped ceramic mug  
sitting cold on the hood.  

This is not awe.  
This is inventory.  
This is counting rivets,  
not constellations.  
This is knowing exactly  
how many seconds pass  
between the last cricket’s chirp  
and the first grain of sand  
shifting under my boot—  
and how, in that silence,  
the dark doesn’t deepen.  
It *settles*.  
Like sediment in a jar of well water  
you’ve stopped shaking.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a jazz club in the rain
text:
A Jazz Club in the Rain

When twilight's gentle fingers stroke the sky,
And rain, like softest whispers, starts to fall,
There lies a club where music never dies,
Its doors wide open, welcoming one and all.

The notes of saxophone, a lover's sigh,
Do mingle with the drumbeat's steady heart,
As shadows dance upon the walls nearby,
In every corner, art gives rise to art.

But lo, what magic doth the rainfall bring?
It paints the night with silver, cool, and bright,
Where lovers' eyes meet under its soft wing,
Their hearts entwined by jazz's tender light.

Though storms may rage without, within we find
A haven, warm, where love and tunes are twined.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a soldier writing home
text:
My Dearest Meg, though ink’s grown thin and blue  
(as if the sky bled through this paper’s grain),  
I write by candle—smoke stings eyes anew,  
and Private Hargrove snores like drowned-out rain.  
This mutton’s tough as boot-leather, I swear—  
yesterday I chewed a gristle for ten minutes—  
and found your last letter tucked inside my spare  
woollen sock, where damp had blurred the “kiss” you printed.  

The poppies here are thick as spilled wine, red  
but not so red as young Tom Bell’s coat-sleeve,  
torn clean at shoulder when the shrapnel sped  
past his ear—still walks, though he won’t believe  
it yet. I saved his pipe, cold and bent,  
and pressed a petal in your letter’s crease.

title: ghazal|learning a second language as an adult
text:
I. The First Word  
My tongue stumbles—foreign, thick, and slow,  
Each syllable a stone I cannot throw.  
The teacher’s voice is clear as mountain air,  
But my own mouth refuses what it knows.  
I write the script with trembling, hopeful hand,  
Yet letters blur like rain on window glass.  
This grammar feels like climbing broken stairs—  
One step up, two steps back—I still confess:  
How strange to beg for meaning, bare and new,  
When silence was my oldest, safest dress.  

II. The Lingering Ghost  
The native phrase blooms sudden in my ear—  
A scent of jasmine I once knew too near.  
My mind supplies the word I meant to say,  
Then catches—*no*, that word is not quite here.  
I dream in fragments, half in English, half  
In verbs that twist and tense without consent.  
My mother-tongue still hums beneath each line,  
A low refrain I cannot quite prevent.  
I name the world twice now—and feel unmoored,  
Like standing where two rivers intersect.  

III. The Unfolding Tongue  
Not fluency, but grace—a slower bloom,  
A quiet light dispelling old dark room.  
I speak and pause—not shame, but sacred space,  
Where listening becomes the truest room.  
The accent stays, a map of where I’ve been,  
Not flaw, but fold where self and language meet.  
One day I laugh mid-sentence, unself-conscious—  
The joke lands whole, both bitter and sweet.  
This tongue is not a copy, sharp and thin—  
It’s mine: worn, warm, and learning how to sing.

title: pantoum|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
The Distant Blaze

Smoke rises, a silent signal in the night,
From far away, the forest whispers pain.
A glow against the darkness, soft yet bright,
The trees stand witness to the fiery rain.

From far away, the forest whispers pain,
Their leaves and branches turned to ash and flame.
The trees stand witness to the fiery rain,
While shadows dance with an eerie, deadly aim.

Their leaves and branches turned to ash and flame,
A glow against the darkness, soft yet bright,
While shadows dance with an eerie, deadly aim,
Smoke rises, a silent signal in the night.

title: blank verse meditation|drought on a family farm
text:
The well’s mouth gapes—not cracked earth, but a rusted  
steel collar, cold to the knuckle, slick with dust  
that tastes like burnt toast and old batteries.  
Grain bins stand hollow, their corrugated skins  
pocked with bullet-holes of rust, each dimple  
holding a single beetle, iridescent, dead.  

I kneel where the alfalfa should be knee-high—  
just stubble, yes, but not golden: gray-green,  
stiff as wire brushes left in rain.  
A jackrabbit freezes mid-leap, then bolts—  
not away, but *around* the same dry pivot  
where the center-pivot arm used to hum,  
now bent at the elbow, its nozzle plugged  
with a wad of tumbleweed, black and knotted  
like a fist full of drowned hair.  

My father’s boots hang on the barn door—  
not for luck, but because the soles dissolved  
in last year’s alkaline puddle, left only  
the uppers, stiff as taxidermied snakeskins,  
laced with twine made from unravelled baling twine.  

At dusk, the wind doesn’t sigh. It *scrapes*:  
a metal file drawn slow across concrete.  
It lifts the topsoil—not in clouds, but in sheets,  
thin as onion skin, translucent enough  
to see the fossilized root-tip of a cottonwood,  
fossilized *upside-down*, pointing skyward  
like a buried finger accusing the empty blue.  

No rain. No prayer. Just the fridge humming  
too loud in the kitchen, its compressor kicking  
on every ninety seconds—cold air leaking  
into the heat, a tiny, stubborn leak,  
like the one in the main line we never fixed,  
the one that hissed for three seasons  
before going silent, leaving only this:  
the weight of the hose reel, empty,  
and the faint, sweet-sour tang of plastic  
baking inside its hollow drum.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
The Humming Vigil  

When sleep’s soft veil refuses to descend,  
And midnight bleeds to gray on hollow walls,  
I lie awake where quiet hours extend—  
No lullaby, no rest, no mercy calls.  
Then from the kitchen, low and unrelenting,  
A steady thrum begins—a muted drone—  
The fridge’s pulse, a ghostly, humming greeting,  
That turns the dark to metal, cold, and stone.  
It does not plead, nor pause, nor ask my leave;  
It simply *is*, as ancient as the stars—  
A monotone that neither lies nor weaves,  
Yet holds me fast beneath its silver bars.  
So I attend this vigil, stark and deep:  
The world sleeps on—I wake with hum and keep.

title: poem in tercets|a mother's hands
text:
Her hands, a map of years, crisscrossed with lines,
Where once they held me, soft as summer peaches,
Now bear the marks of time's relentless grind.

In kitchen light, her fingers dance on dough,
Kneading life into each ball and roll, the scent
Of yeast and warmth, a childhood I still know.

She sorts through photos, yellowed at the edges,
Tracing faces with a touch so light, it seems
To whisper secrets only she can pledge.

When illness came, those hands grew frail, yet strong—
A paradox of tenderness and steel,
Holding mine, a silent, steadfast song.

I see her garden, earth beneath her nails,
Tomatoes ripe, and roses in full bloom,
Each petal tended, every weed that wails.

And in the night, when shadows stretch and loom,
Her hands, a comfort, stroke my hair, a balm,
A lullaby, a shelter from the gloom.

title: prose poem|a beekeeper in winter
text:
The Beekeeper in Winter  

He stands at the edge of the apiary, breath pluming like a small, lost hive. The hives are mounds of snow-draped silence—white shrouds over black wood, each lid weighted with frost, each entrance sealed by ice-glazed propolis. Inside, the bees are not sleeping; they are *holding*. A slow, dense cluster around the queen, trembling—not with cold, but with the ancient calculus of heat: wing-muscles flexing, shivering into warmth, passing it hand-to-hand, mouth-to-mouth, thorax-to-thorax, a living furnace banked low beneath the winter’s iron sky.  

His gloves are stiff with beeswax and cold. He presses a palm to the northern wall of Hive Three—not to open, never to disturb—but to feel the hum. Not sound, not vibration, but *presence*: a subsonic thrumming in the bone, the quiet pulse of life refusing erasure. Frost feathers his eyebrows. His beard holds tiny crystals, each one a captured breath, a suspended note.  

He remembers summer: the gold-dust air, the furious geometry of flight, the sting that bloomed hot and sudden on his wrist—a sacrament of attention. Now, the only gold is the honey he decanted last October, thick and amber in glass jars on the cellar shelf, glowing like captured sunset. It will feed them through February. It will feed *him*, too—when he stirs a spoonful into weak tea, the sweetness so deep it aches, a reminder that sweetness is not the absence of cold, but its tender, tenacious counterweight.  

At dusk, he walks back past the frozen creek, where the water moves unseen beneath the ice—dark, insistent, singing its low song to the roots. He does not pray. He watches. He waits. And in the stillness between one breath and the next, he hears it: not the buzz of wings, but the almost-sound of survival—soft as down, steady as gravity—keeping time with the earth’s slow turn toward light.

title: ghazal|the stars seen from a desert
text:
Desert Stars

The dunes exhale their ancient, silver sigh—  
each star a needle stitching night’s deep sky.  

No roof but void, no wall but wind’s low chant—  
the stars descend where thirsty camels lie.  

They do not blink—they burn with patient fire,  
cold lamps hung where lost caravans pass by.  

I named them once; they answered not my voice—  
just spun their light on dust and time and dry.  

My heart, a well with no reflection left,  
still holds the stars it cannot quench or buy.  

O constellations—do you know my name?  
Or am I just the dark you pierce and fly?

title: ode|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
In the quiet hum of fluorescent lights,
where shadows stretch like tired limbs,
she steps from the ward, her sneakers
whispering secrets to the linoleum.

Her scrubs, a canvas of accidental art—
ink smudges bloom like midnight violets,
a coffee stain maps an uncharted continent,
and the creases hold stories only she can read.

At the locker, her hands move with the grace
of a locksmith, each turn a ritual, a release.
The metal door swings open, a portal
to another world where the air is thick
with the scent of lavender and pine.

She peels off layers, each one a skin
shed in the heat of battle, until she stands
in the soft armor of street clothes,
a warrior disguised as a civilian.

Outside, the night wraps its cool arms
around her, and the stars blink like IV monitors,
steady, watchful. She walks through the parking lot,
her footsteps a syncopated rhythm,
a heartbeat that echoes through the city.

In her car, the dashboard glows softly,
a lighthouse in the dark, guiding her home.
The engine purrs, a cat curling at her feet,
and she drives, the road unwinding
like a long, deep breath, a sigh of relief.

title: villanelle|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
The Garden After the Gardener’s Death

The roses climb where no hand prunes the vine,  
The path is lost beneath the tangled green,  
No voice calls names to coax the stems to twine.  

The gate hangs crooked, rusted on its line,  
While daisies crowd the stone where once was seen  
The roses climb where no hand prunes the vine.  

The fountain sleeps, its basin choked with silt and brine,  
No water sings—the dry stone holds no sheen—  
No voice calls names to coax the stems to twine.  

The hollyhocks stand tall, then lean, decline,  
Their purple heads bow low where shadows lean;  
The roses climb where no hand prunes the vine.  

A sparrow nests inside the gardener’s hat, left behind,  
Its straw now frayed, its shape half-soft, half-thin—  
No voice calls names to coax the stems to twine.  

Though time unspools what love so tightly bound,  
The soil remembers every seed it’s been:  
The roses climb where no hand prunes the vine,  
No voice calls names to coax the stems to twine.

title: ballad in quatrains|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The porch swing’s rusted chain still groans  
like it did when I’d kick off my shoes,  
but the floorboard by the door—third from left—  
still squeaks the same damn tune, not news.  

Mom’s chipped mug’s gone from the cupboard shelf,  
but the stain’s still there, brown and thin,  
where she spilled chamomile every Tuesday  
while pretending the rent wasn’t due in.  

I packed the box marked “Dad’s Things”  
with one shirt, a bent spoon, his watch—  
stopped at 3:17, the day he walked out,  
not the day he came back, not quite.  

The lilacs by the fence are scraggly now,  
pruned wrong, half-drowned in clay,  
but their smell hit me sharp this morning—  
wet dirt, bruised petals, yesterday.  

The key’s cold in my palm, too small,  
fits the lock but won’t turn twice.  
I left it in the bowl by the stove,  
next to the loose button, the dried-up ice.

title: short lyric poem|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
In the city's quiet hum, a bus rolls by,
At two a.m., beneath the moonlit sky.
Its windows glow, like lanterns in the night,
Each pane a story, softly burning bright.

The driver's gaze, a steady, silent stream,
Guides through the shadows, as if in a dream.
Passengers few, each wrapped in thoughts so deep,
Their breaths like whispers, secrets they might keep.

Streets stretch ahead, in silver and in blue,
A canvas vast, with every hue anew.
The wheels, they sing a lullaby so low,
To all the souls who've found a place to go.

And as it fades, into the distant light,
A gentle peace descends, as soft as night.
For in its wake, this city bus bestows
A moment's calm, where only quiet flows.

title: short lyric poem|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Friday Light  
The bleachers exhale dust and sweat,  
a thousand voices hum low—  
not quite song, not quite prayer—  
as the sun dips behind the pines.  
A whistle cuts the amber air.  
Someone’s mother adjusts her son’s collar,  
her fingers trembling just once.  

Third Quarter  
Grass stains bloom on white jerseys,  
helmets gleam like wet river stones.  
The quarterback stumbles, rises,  
spits grass and grins.  
A boy in the front row clutches his father’s cap,  
too small for the roar, too big to look away.  
The scoreboard flickers: 14–10.  
Time bends, thick as honey.  

After the Whistle  
Lights blaze cold now, emptying fast—  
paper cups swirl in the wind,  
a lone glove lies abandoned near the goalpost.  
Two teams shake hands, helmets under arms,  
faces streaked with mud and something softer.  
Somewhere, a radio plays static and a distant game.  
We walk home slow,  
carrying the echo like a shared secret.

title: villanelle|grief after a dog dies
text:
The leash still hangs by the back door’s rusted hinge,  
a coiled question mark no one answers now.  
Your water bowl’s a shallow, dust-rimmed thing.  

I found your favorite sock beneath the fridge—  
still warm where fur once snagged the rubber sole.  
The leash still hangs by the back door’s rusted hinge.  

At dusk, the neighbor’s terrier barks, and I flinch  
like a nerve exposed, raw in the thinning air.  
Your water bowl’s a shallow, dust-rimmed thing.  

The vet’s receipt curls at the edge of the counter:  
*Euthanasia, sedation, cremation fee.*  
The leash still hangs by the back door’s rusted hinge.  

I vacuumed twice today—just to hear the hum,  
the only sound that doesn’t name your name.  
Your water bowl’s a shallow, dust-rimmed thing.  

Last night, I dreamed you were a cracked sidewalk,  
warm asphalt yielding under my bare feet.  
The leash still hangs by the back door’s rusted hinge.  
Your water bowl’s a shallow, dust-rimmed thing.

title: spoken-word poem|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
A Library on a Sunday Afternoon

In the hush of pages turned, in whispers soft and light,
Where time itself seems to pause, to bask in gentle quiet,
Sits the library, a sanctuary of thoughts unspoken,
A harbor for dreams, under the watch of book spines broken.

Here, where the sun's fingers stretch, lazy and long,
Casting shadows that dance upon stories strong,
Patrons wander, like silent specters of old,
Seeking solace in tales, bold and cold.

The air is thick with the scent of ink and paper,
A fragrance that clings, an eternal caper.
Each breath taken, a sip from the well of knowledge,
Nourishing minds, in this haven of silence and college.

Children, eyes wide with wonder, explore realms afar,
Their imaginations sparked by each word, like a star.
Elders, too, find comfort in familiar lines,
Reliving memories, through verses that shine.

Outside, the world rushes, in chaos and noise,
But within these walls, there's only the choice
To lose oneself in the magic, the mystery, the might,
Of words penned down, in black and white.

As afternoon fades into evening's embrace,
This temple of wisdom remains in its place,
A beacon for those who seek understanding and peace,
In the heart of the city, where all worries cease.

title: sequence of haiku|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
First snow—  
the cracked asphalt gleams  
under sodium light.  

My coffee cup’s lid  
still says “St. Vincent’s”  
faded blue, chipped rim.  

That kid in 3B  
left footprints dragging  
toward the bus stop.  

Wind lifts a single glove  
from the overflow lot—  
blue, small, missing fingers.  

Snow on the ER awning  
melts slow, then drips  
onto the “No Loitering” sign.

title: sequence of haiku|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
Subway Sequence  

Steel throat exhales steam—  
a thousand breaths condense, then fade—  
my coat brushes yours.  

Neon bleeds through glass—  
a woman’s earbuds pulse low;  
her knuckles whiten.  

Rain-streaked tunnel dark—  
the train sways, a tired spine—  
we hold the same pole.  

A child points: *Look! Light!*  
and for three stops, we are air—  
then doors sigh open.

title: dramatic monologue|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
Rust Psalm

The whistle’s gone. Not broken—*gone*.  
No iron lung to heave the dawn,  
no steam-hiss hymn to stitch the gray,  
no clang of gears that marked the day.  
Just silence—thick as factory dust,  
settled deep in every crust  
of brick and bone and boarded glass,  
where time itself has ground to pass.

I walk the street where men once marched  
in grease-stained boots, shoulders arched—  
not proud, but *known*: the lathe-man, welder,  
foreman’s nod, the shift’s slow elder.  
Now windows gape like hollow eyes,  
their panes all starred with shattered skies.  
The smokestack stands—a blackened spine,  
a monument to what was *mine*,  
to what was *ours*, to what we built  
with calloused hands and sleepless guilt  
for wages thin and futures thin,  
while hope ran low and bosses grinned.

The diner’s open—barely—light  
a single bulb, too weak, too white.  
Marla pours coffee, cold and thin,  
and doesn’t ask who’s left within.  
She knows. We all do. Names erased  
from payrolls, then from memory’s space:  
Joe’s truck’s been sold, his daughter fled  
to Atlanta, beds unmade, unread  
college brochures on the floor.  
Maggie’s still here—she cleans the store  
that sells no goods but ghosts and glue,  
and hums a tune she can’t get through.

Some nights I stand beneath that stack,  
press palm to rust—still warm, not slack—  
as if the furnace breathes below,  
a phantom heat no one will know.  
But it’s just wind through broken vents,  
the town’s last sigh, its slow descent  
into the hush where engines slept,  
where promises were over-kept,  
where children learn the alphabet  
from faded signs: *“Quality. Integrity. Growth.”*  
All rusted out. All stripped. All lost.  

We don’t rage. Not anymore.  
We just hold the quiet door—  
and wait for something new to rise,  
or for the silence to grow wise.

title: blank verse meditation|grief after a dog dies
text:
After the Last Walk  

The leash still hangs beside the back door—  
a coil of worn nylon, stiff with dried mud,  
its brass clasp dulled, its buckle cold to touch.  
I reach for it each morning, then pause,  
my hand suspended in the quiet air,  
as if the weight of habit might still summon  
the soft thud of paws on linoleum,  
the eager whine before the latch clicks up.  

The house is too large now, too still.  
No warm weight pressed against my knee at dusk,  
no nose nudging my wrist for a scratch behind the ear—  
just silence, thick and unrelenting,  
filling corners where her shadow used to pool.  

I find her hair caught in the bristles of the brush,  
a tangle of gold and gray, fine as spun light.  
I hold it—not to keep, but to remember  
how it caught the sun when she ran,  
how it softened under my palm when she slept,  
how it drifted, weightless, from her coat  
in the weeks before the vet’s hushed voice,  
before the final, gentle letting go.  

Grief is not a storm—it is the slow seep of tide  
into dry sand: quiet, inevitable,  
leaving hollows no filling can restore.  
I do not weep for what is gone,  
but for the ordinary miracles I mistook for given:  
the way she waited, always,  
not for treats or praise, but for *me*—  
for my breath, my step, my return.  
She loved without condition,  
lived without pretense,  
died without ceremony—  
and in that simple, faithful brevity,  
taught me how deeply love can root  
in the small, unremarkable earth of daily things.  

So I walk alone now,  
but carry her pace inside me—  
a rhythm beneath my ribs,  
a warmth where her head once rested,  
a quiet certainty:  
some bonds do not end with breath,  
but deepen, unseen,  
like roots in dark soil,  
holding the ground together  
long after the green has faded.

title: spoken-word poem|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
In the shadow of smokestacks, now cold and gray,
Echoes of hammers, silence fills the day.
Rusty gates hang open, like mouths agape,
Whispering secrets of a time that escaped.

Old man Jenkins, he used to walk with pride,
Wore his coveralls like a badge, chest wide.
Now he shuffles, eyes down, hands in pockets deep,
Searching for coins, or maybe just sleep.

The diner’s empty, save for Betty's frown,
Coffee grows stale, her dreams are brown.
She talks to ghosts, sips from cracked mugs,
Remembers laughter, but can't find the hugs.

Kids on the street, no future in sight,
Chalk drawings on pavement, their only light.
Factory playground, twisted metal and rust,
A jungle gym for the lost, the forgotten, the just.

Even the river, once blue, now gray,
Carries the town’s sorrows, day by day.
Fish float belly up, and the ducks have flown,
Leaving behind a mirror, showing what we’ve grown.

At night, the stars still shine, indifferent, cold,
As if they’ve seen this story, a hundred times told.
But in the dark, there’s a flicker, a spark,
Maybe it’s hope, or maybe just heart.

title: sequence of haiku|watching a parent grow old
text:
Sequence of Haiku: Watching You Grow Old  

First light—  
your hand trembles holding the teacup,  
steam rising like breath.  

Winter window—  
frost etches fragile branches  
on the glass you wipe.  

Your glasses fog—  
you peer at my face, then smile,  
mistaking my name.  

Folded sweater—  
sleeves too long, wool soft as down,  
still smelling of lavender.  

Empty chair—  
the newspaper lies open,  
page turned by wind.

title: dramatic monologue|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
I. The Last Stop Before Dawn  
The engine hums a low, tired hymn,  
headlights slicing fog like dull knives—  
no one boards but the rain,  
and the ghost of a man who checks his watch  
then vanishes into the wet brick wall.  
I steer the empty aisle,  
fingers white on the wheel’s cold rim,  
while the fare box clicks open and shut,  
open and shut,  
though no coin has dropped in hours.

II. The One Who Rides the Line  
She sits behind me, third row left,  
coat too thin for this hour,  
staring at her reflection in the black window—  
not seeing herself, but something moving just beyond the glass:  
a flicker, a shadow with no source.  
She whispers to the seat beside her,  
names I don’t recognize,  
and when she stands to exit,  
her breath fogs the glass in the shape of a door.  
I don’t look back.  
I never do.

III. Terminal Silence  
The depot lights buzz like trapped wasps.  
I kill the engine.  
The bus sighs—air brakes exhale,  
doors wheeze shut,  
and for three breaths, it is still:  
no radio static, no distant siren,  
just the slow drip of condensation  
from the roof vent onto the floor mat.  
Then the radio crackles—  
*“Driver, you’re clear for layover.”*  
I don’t answer.  
I rest my forehead on the wheel  
and count the seconds until the next shift begins,  
until the city remembers it needs us again.

title: dramatic monologue|the ocean during a storm
text:
The Ocean's Fury

Beneath the shroud of night, I rise and swell,
A titan clad in tempests, waves my crest.
I roar with voices old as time itself,
And in my heart, a storm that knows no rest.

The heavens weep their tears into my depths,
As lightning scythes the sky with fiery hands.
My breath is wind, a howling, bitter song,
That shatters ships and scatters ocean sands.

Oh, hear me, land-dwellers, in your safety,
For I am chaos, I am fear, I am might.
No anchor holds, no lighthouse pierces through,
When I, the sea, decide to claim the night.

The gulls have fled, the dolphins seek the deep,
But I, undaunted, rage against the shore.
My fury builds, a crescendo of despair,
Till every soul on earth shall know my roar.

Yet in my wrath, there lies a mournful plea,
To be understood, to not be feared, but known.
For even oceans long for peace at times,
In storms, we find our strength, and then are grown.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|time and memory
text:
Sonnet for the Clock That Swallowed My Keys  

The second hand gnaws rust from iron hinges—  
not metaphor, but actual flakes that fall  
like dandruff off a rusted bicycle chain  
I left last spring behind the garage wall.  

My mother’s voice arrives via landline static:  
a dial tone hums beneath her “How are you?”  
as if the wire itself remembers  
the exact pitch of her laugh, worn thin and true.  

That photo—faded at the corners, bent—  
shows me knee-deep in creek-muck, grinning,  
holding a crayfish whose claws still pinch  
the air between thumb and forefinger,  
though the creature’s long dissolved to silt.  

Time isn’t sand. It’s the fridge light’s buzz  
that stays on after the door’s shut—  
a small, persistent voltage in the dark,  
humming the shape of what was,  
but not quite *what*.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
The light slants low—three o’clock, maybe four—  
and hits the dust motes dancing over Dewey.  
I’m in 821.3 again, though I swore  
I’d skip the Victorians today. My knee  
aches where the old splinter dug in, back  
in ’09, prying loose that warped floorboard  
behind the microfiche reader (still black  
and humming faintly, like a tired chord).  
Mrs. Gable’s knitting needles click-clack  
near the biography shelves—blue yarn, slow pace.  
A kid drops a volume of Auden; it cracks  
like dry twigs underfoot. No one looks up.  
The radiator hisses steam, then sighs.  
I trace the watermark on this page—half-erased,  
a ghostly lily, pressed by someone’s thumb  
who never signed their name, just left it there.

title: elegy|drought on a family farm
text:
Beneath the sun's relentless, scorching eye,
The fields lie barren, earth as cracked and dry
As ancient parchment, whispering of loss.
No verdant life, no green to comfort us.

The once proud stalks, now withered, pale, and thin,
Stand like the ghosts of seasons long since spun.
Their leaves, a brittle memory, cling on
To stems that bend beneath the weight of none.

The well, our lifeline, silent, deep, and still,
Reflects the sky, a mirror to despair.
Its waters, once so plentiful, now shrill,
A mocking echo of what used to be there.

Our hands, calloused, worn from endless toil,
Reach out in vain to skies too blue, too vast.
Each cloud that forms, then fades, without recoil,
Leaves in its wake a sorrow that will last.

The old barn stands, a sentinel of time,
Its weathered boards a testament to years
Of laughter, tears, and stories left behind,
Now shadows dance where once was joyous cheer.

At dusk, the horizon paints a mournful scene,
A palette of reds and oranges, fierce, yet cold.
It speaks of endings, of what might have been,
A canvas splashed with dreams that never hold.

And in the night, when stars pierce through the dark,
We gather 'round, our hearts both heavy, light.
In whispered tones, we share the day's stark mark,
And find in silence, strength to face the night.

title: poem in tercets|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
I. Arrival  
The sky unspools its gray and thin,  
a hush descends—not silence, but the weight  
of waiting held between breaths and skin.  

II. Landing  
Flakes alight on windshields, cold and slight,  
on gurney wheels, on cigarette ash,  
on the cracked asphalt where light  
refuses to stay—too frail, too brief, too rash.  

III. After  
A child’s glove lies half-buried, blue and small,  
a nurse pauses, breath pluming, then walks on—  
the lot now soft, white, holding nothing at all.

title: blank verse meditation|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
Midnight Transit

The engine hums—a low and steady thrum—  
a pulse beneath the floorboards, worn and thin.  
No driver speaks; his gaze stays fixed ahead,  
where sodium lights smear yellow on the wet street.  
A woman nods against the fogged-up glass,  
her coat pulled tight, a grocery bag slack  
beside her boots. Her breath fogs, fades, returns.  

Two youths sit close but do not touch—  
one scrolls a screen’s cold glow across his face,  
the other stares past rows of empty seats,  
past ads for things no one buys at this hour:  
vacations, loans, bright teeth, quick fixes—all  
unreal as mist that gathers on the windows.  

The bus lurches, brakes sigh, a pause too long—  
then rolls again through blocks of shuttered shops,  
past fire escapes like ribs against brick walls,  
past alleys where the wind stirs crumpled paper,  
past stoops where silence settles, thick and deep,  
as if the city holds its breath between dreams.  

No sirens now. No shouts. Just rain’s soft tap  
on roof and glass, the rhythm of the wipers,  
left-right, left-right—the only conversation.  
We move through sleep like ghosts inside a shell,  
carried forward—not toward home, not yet,  
but through the hush where time itself slows down,  
and every soul aboard becomes a thought  
the city thinks, then lets go, softly, on.

title: sequence of haiku|the sound of a train at night
text:
Steel whispers through dark,  
City's heartbeat fades, distant—  
Tracks hum lullabies.

Night air stirs, alive,  
Vibrations cradle the moonlight—  
Whispers of departure.

Rumbling bass notes dance,  
Neon signs flicker in sync—  
Silent buildings sway.

title: prose poem|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
First Gear  

The car is a nervous animal, engine humming low in the driveway’s quiet. He adjusts the seat—not too far, not too close—his hand steady on the wheel as if holding a bird that might startle. She grips the rim, knuckles pale, breath shallow. “Eyes up,” he says, not unkindly, and she lifts her gaze from the hood to the empty street ahead, where dandelions push through cracked asphalt like tiny, stubborn stars. He guides her hands: ten and two, not nine and three, because he remembers his own father saying, *This is how you hold something precious without squeezing it dry*. The clutch bites, the engine stutters, the car lurches forward—then stalls. She flinches. He doesn’t sigh. He turns the key again, soft and sure. “Again,” he says, and means *again*, not *try harder*, not *don’t fail*. Her foot finds the pedal’s resistance, her shoulders drop an inch, her left hand releases just enough to let the wheel breathe. They roll past the oak where he once scraped his first fender, past the mailbox painted with chipped blue letters, past the neighbor’s dog who barks but doesn’t chase. No destination. Just this: the hum, the light on the dash, the way her reflection in the windshield holds his eyes for a second—steady, startled, already learning how to carry the weight of motion, how to steer not just metal and glass, but the quiet, trembling space between instruction and trust.
